audit.lens: Science of ML evaluation and benchmarking (leakage, splits, hidden tests, statistics, metric validity, construct validity, ceilings, documentation, freezing, Goodhart, adoption), applied to plan/plan.md and section id="next" of page/big-picture.html. Sourcing note: in THIS run I opened only six web pages: Post 2018 (arxiv.org/abs/1804.08771), Miller 2024 (arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640, abstract only; the abstract does not name clustering), Ribeiro et al. 2020 CheckList (arxiv.org/abs/2005.04118), the Dara paper HTML (arxiv.org/html/2510.19667), the RADAR-PD paper HTML (arxiv.org/html/2605.12478), and the GALAXI abstract (arxiv.org/abs/2609.06908). Pages were read through a summarising fetch tool, so re-check exact wording before quoting in public. Every other source named below was opened by the stage-1 compiler, not by me: treat as opened=false for this run. Nothing was downloaded, no form filled, nobody contacted, no file written.

is_eval_work.which_parts_are_eval: Almost all of it, and mostly META-evaluation (testing the tests, not the models). D1, N1, L1 = metric validity and versioning (is the scoring rule right and stable). D3, N2 = leakage and grouped splits. D4 = error bars and paired comparison. D6, N3, L2, L5 = test-set construction and hidden-test governance. N4 = ceilings (best achievable score). N5 = a benchmark-trust checklist. Inside D2, only the private check 'does a duplicate sit on both sides of my calibration/test split' is eval. The early project decision was explicit: 'evaluation data before a training corpus' (synth/storyline.md:63). So the user's instinct is right, and checking against eval principles first is a fair ask.
is_eval_work.which_parts_are_not: D0 file rescue = housekeeping. D5 and L3 (error notes to dataset owners) and L4 (neutral notice about 499 matching files) = data-error reporting and curation courtesy. N6 (flag-only suspect list) = data-quality tooling. Most of D2 = a data provenance audit: by the plan's own correction 12 (plan/plan.md:177) the 499 files carry no answer label, so they cannot inflate a test score. The critique of one company's 134-item test is an application of eval statistics, not a plan item. Honest framing for the user: every item before L2 audits existing exams. Only L2 creates new test data, and L2 needs a lab.
is_eval_work.best_one_line_name_for_this_work: Meta-evaluation for materials ML on measured data: auditing how the exams are set, marked and sized, before trying to build a new one.

scorecard.principle: Split by the unit that leaks
scorecard.evidence: plan/plan.md:88 D3 writes a frozen list of test DOIs (paper IDs) with a checksum and 'a 30-line leak report (X% of test rows have a sibling in training)'. plan/plan.md:184 (correction 17) says most of the 25.5-to-42.2 jump is unseen formulas. plan/plan.md:186 (correction 19): a chemical-system holdout still leaves the test paper in training 52.4% of the time. plan/plan.md:85 D2: 'does any duplicate pair sit on both sides of your calibration/test split?'. synth/gaps.md:208: the 40 scans are 20 mixtures, each scanned for 2 and 8 minutes. synth/builds.md:351: the user's project uses the Dara benchmark among its datasets.
scorecard.gap: The leak report names one sibling key. The plan's own correction says formula novelty, not paper identity, drives most of the jump, so one key cannot explain the number. D2 checks exact duplicate files only. A 2-minute and an 8-minute scan of the same powder are not duplicates but are siblings. Whether the user's project keeps them on one side of its calibration/test split is unknown.
scorecard.fix: D3 leak report prints two lines: share of test rows with a same-paper sibling in train (must be 0 on the paper split) and share with a same-formula sibling (reported, with the seen/unseen breakdown kept beside every number). D2's private check also groups by powder (mixture ID), not only by file hash. N2 cites Meredig et al. 2018 and Kapoor and Narayanan 2022 for the general claim and claims only the TE numbers and the frozen list (both opened by stage 1, not by me).

scorecard.principle: Freeze test list and decision rule first
scorecard.evidence: Good: plan/plan.md:110 'Fix in advance which bands count as harder'; plan/plan.md:104 dated amendment before touching the pre-registered project; plan/plan.md:88 frozen DOI list with checksum. Not good: plan/plan.md:30 'Hand-sort each into spelling artifact or real chemistry disagreement' has no written definition of either bin. plan/plan.md:36 'One written line says either reusable marker is worth building or this is a bug-fix' has no threshold. plan/plan.md:23: the sorter's own pilot moves 0.309 to 0.745 with the rule, so the sorter has a stake. plan/plan.md:79 says a formula-only marker must be allowed 'cannot tell', yet the hand-sort has only two bins. plan/plan.md:184: 1-neighbour vs 5-neighbour was compared on test numbers. plan/plan.md:107: N2's new baseline runs 'under all three splits' with no dev split.
scorecard.gap: The first step ends in a verdict with no pre-set rule, judged by an interested party, using undefined categories. This is the one thing that cannot be repaired after the rows have been seen. 12, 17 and 32 are already known, so reproducing them is a sanity check, not a finding; the only new measurement is the hand-sort count.
scorecard.fix: Before opening the project folders, write a dated half-page protocol and hash it. (a) Three bins with written definitions and two worked examples each from notes already seen: spelling artifact (same compound, different string, e.g. Ni1.875O2 vs NiO), real chemistry disagreement (different ideal ratio or compound, e.g. Nb2O5 vs Nb12O29), cannot tell from formula alone. (b) A three-way rule with a grey zone, for example: residual rows = rows still marked differently after a fixed, written formula clean-up; 2 or fewer of 40 = 'bug-fix'; 8 or more = 'real on this set'; in between = 'undecided on 40 rows, decide after re-marking N3'. The exact numbers are the user's call; what matters is that they are written first. (c) State counts in powders (20) as well as scans (40). Later, for N2: cut a dev set of papers out of the training papers, choose neighbour count and tree settings on dev only, and report 1-neighbour and 5-neighbour side by side.
scorecard.effort: 1 hour now; half a day for the TE dev split later

scorecard.principle: Intervals that respect clusters; compare paired
scorecard.evidence: plan/plan.md:90-91 D4 'prints an interval and a tie / not a tie verdict... 38 of 40 vs 35 of 40 must return tie'. No cluster or paired argument in the spec. page/big-picture.html:499 already says 'paired gap' and 'The 40 scans are really 20 powders, each scanned twice', so the knowledge is there but not in the function. synth/builds.md:702: 'row-level confidence intervals on clustered data were wrong. Method rule now: ... count clusters (papers, runs)'. plan/plan.md:91 says D1 calls D4 'by default', but D4 is scheduled after D1.
scorecard.gap: The function as specified would repeat an error the notes already recorded once. TE rows cluster by paper (12,222 rows, 3,015 papers).
scorecard.fix: Spec: tie_or_not(scores_a, scores_b=None, cluster_id=None, paired=True). Resample clusters (powders, papers), not rows. Use an exact paired test (McNemar) for small yes/no sets. Three tests: 38 vs 35 of 40 with 20 clusters returns 'tie'; strict-vs-lenient on the 18 tricky pairs is reported as a paired comparison (my arithmetic: the exact paired p-value is 0.06 at best, only if every disagreement runs one way, so it is probably a tie); one TE case resampled by paper. Cite Miller 2024 (abstract opened this run; clustering is in the body, which I did not open) and Dietterich 1998 (not opened). Claim no novelty. Write D4 before D1's write-up.
scorecard.effort: the budgeted half day plus 1 hour

scorecard.principle: Size the test before building it
scorecard.evidence: Follows for L2: plan/plan.md:127 'about 385 separate powders for plus or minus 5 points near 50% accuracy; about 470-780 paired powders'; plan/plan.md:196 (correction 27) reconciles paired vs unpaired. Follows for N3 on the page: page/big-picture.html:511 'If the hard bands hold far fewer than about 385 separate powders, the practice exam can describe difficulty but cannot rank tools'; plan/plan.md:110 'not a ranking of tools'. Missing for D1 and N2.
scorecard.gap: D1 never says what 40 rows can detect. My arithmetic: 5 residual rows of 40 gives a 95% interval of roughly 5% to 26% before clustering, and wider with 20 powders. So D1 can tell 'almost none' from 'many' and nothing finer. N2 has no sizing for its three-split comparison by paper.
scorecard.fix: One sentence in the D1 protocol: '40 rows on 20 powders cannot fix prevalence to better than about plus or minus 10 points; hence a three-way verdict'. Optional, no new access needed: hand-sort the 18 rule-dependent rows among the 210 pilot rows (synth/gaps.md:153) as a second sheet. After D6, write each band's powder count and the interval it gives before asking for any download.

scorecard.principle: Give the metric a signature and version
scorecard.evidence: plan/plan.md:164 (correction 1): three causes of the spread = rule, stale stored marks, reference library and set-up. plan/plan.md:29: three marks per scan (strict as stored, lenient as stored, lenient recomputed). plan/plan.md:34: about 15 stale rows in a 56-row file. plan/plan.md:104: N1 runner 're-marks a results file under every rule', no settings string. page/big-picture.html:474 already names sacreBLEU, but only as the twin of the unit-test file. Web, opened this run: the Dara paper counts a scan correct if it 'includes all precursor phases ... and excludes any spurious phases' (arxiv.org/html/2510.19667); RADAR-PD counts a sample correct 'if any predicted candidate matched any trusted reference label', judged by a GPT-4 prompt (arxiv.org/html/2605.12478); GALAXI reports micro-F1 0.935 with no matching rule in its abstract (arxiv.org/abs/2609.06908). Three papers, three units.
scorecard.gap: No stored score in the plan carries its settings. Correction 1's three causes are exactly three signature fields. Without a stamp, 'lenient recomputed' becomes the next stale mark.
scorecard.fix: Add one signature string per mark to the 40-row table: rule name and code hash, tolerance (0.10), formula clean-up version, Dara version (1.1.12), reference library and snapshot date, candidate cap (80), what 'correct' means at scan level (exact set / any match / per phase), date computed. Extend the done-test: 'each of 12, 17, 32 and the paper's 38 is explained by naming which signature fields differ'. Cite Post 2018, A Call for Clarity in Reporting BLEU Scores, https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.08771 (opened this run: scores differ by up to 1.8 between common configurations; the tool enforces one scheme).

scorecard.principle: Check the metric against expert judgment
scorecard.evidence: Follows: plan/plan.md:78 'AI-drafted, not yet reviewed by a specialist' and 'disagrees with the draft key, not wrong'. plan/plan.md:125 L1: one specialist, 'One specialist cannot settle every tier'. page/big-picture.html:614 adds 'About 10 unseen pairs, as a held-out check that the rule was not tuned to the table'; plan.md lacks that line. plan/plan.md:30: the hand-sort is a single pass by a newcomer plus an AI. RADAR-PD page (opened this run) reports no check of its GPT-4 judge against people.
scorecard.gap: The hand-sort is itself a labelling task and has no agreement measure. One rater at L1 gives no agreement number either.
scorecard.fix: D1: two blind passes over the differing rows (for example two separate AI sessions that see only the written bin definitions and the two formula strings, not each other's output and not the hoped-for answer). Report raw agreement. The rows where the passes differ become the first rows shown to a specialist. Label the verdict line 'draft, not specialist-reviewed'. L1 later: ask for two specialists working apart if possible; if only one, write 'one rater, no agreement figure'. Copy the '10 unseen pairs' line into plan.md.

scorecard.principle: Say what decision the score supports
scorecard.evidence: plan/plan.md:104: tiered marker (same / spelled differently / same family, different crystal form / different / cannot tell / specialists disagree) is the right shape. plan/plan.md:165 (correction 2): the rule moves 12 vs 32 of 40 on weighed mixtures but only 1 to 3 of 20 on reaction products, where the tool gap is 11 to 13. plan/plan.md:107: TE note adds sign accuracy and absolute error (follows). plan/plan.md:36: the D1 verdict rests on the 40 weighed scans only.
scorecard.gap: No preset names a user and a decision. The D1 verdict is drawn on the sample type where tools tie; on the type nearer real lab use the rule barely mattered.
scorecard.fix: Now: append to the D1 verdict line 'on weighed mixtures in my set-up; on 20 reaction products the rule moved 1-3 of 20'. At N1: one line per preset, 'user / decision / tiers that count as correct'. In the L2 draft: one line saying weighed mixtures of bought powders test a narrower skill than reaction products, and whether one predicts the other is unknown.
scorecard.effort: 10 minutes now; the rest at N1

scorecard.principle: Show floor, ceiling and headroom
scorecard.evidence: Follows on TE: plan/plan.md:113 five-rung ladder, each rung with an 'includes / excludes' line, and 'The across-paper spread is not pure noise'. Follows on pruning: plan/plan.md:146 dropped the relabelled set for no headroom (random 20.1% vs perfect 21.8%); plan/plan.md:91 treats 38 vs 35 as a tie. Missing on X-ray: plan/plan.md:110 N3 has bands and a candidate-list flag but no floor and no ceiling; plan/plan.md:127 L2 sizing assumes accuracy near 50%.
scorecard.gap: The X-ray side has no ladder. L2's sizing rests on an unconfirmed 50%.
scorecard.fix: N3 table adds, per band: a trivial floor ('name only the major ingredients'), a ceiling line (lab scans cannot see ingredients below roughly 1 to 5% by weight per the stage-1 notes, unverified by me; plus human-analyst results from the old round-robin reports if D6 finds them), and Dara. Do not send the L2 request until N3 shows hard-band accuracy is far from both 0 and 100. N4 cites Crusius, Cipcigan, Biggin 2025 (not opened by anyone: 403) and checks their package before writing new code.

scorecard.principle: A hidden test needs rules, not just secrecy
scorecard.evidence: plan/plan.md:127 one-page request lists 'how many powders, pilot size, file-naming rule (today's file names spell out the recipe), who holds the answers' and states 'a one-instrument exam'. plan/plan.md:141 'Using datasets with public answers as a hidden test. Refuted. Practice exam only' (follows). synth/gaps.md:210 records the file-name leak.
scorecard.gap: Missing: a cap on scored submissions, a refresh plan, a hashed answer key, a rule that the custodian does not enter, and what gets published afterwards.
scorecard.fix: Add five lines to the L2 draft: custodian does not enter a tool; answer-key hash lodged before release; at most N scored submissions per tool per round; new powders each round, old ones become the practice exam; file names and file headers scrubbed of recipe clues. Models: CASP; Blum and Hardt 2015; Jacovi et al. 2023 (all opened by stage 1, not by me).
scorecard.effort: 1 hour, when the one-pager is drafted

scorecard.principle: Ship a datasheet with every artefact
scorecard.evidence: Pieces exist: plan/plan.md:28 content hashes; :78 a label column saying 'AI-drafted'; :85 neutral wording ('identical to', never 'copied from'); :88 snapshot name, checksum, DOIs only; :155 IDs and hashes only for unlicensed data. No common template. plan/plan.md:116 N5 does not map onto existing general checklists.
scorecard.gap: Scattered hygiene, no single sheet. N5 risks re-stating REFORMS (32 questions) and BetterBench (46 criteria) as if new.
scorecard.fix: One 8-field header pasted on top of every CSV from D1 onward: source snapshot and hash; how rows were chosen; who or what made the labels; licence; known errors; not-for uses (for example 'not a hidden test', 'hand-picked, not a prevalence sample'); metric signature; date. N5 maps each of its four questions to REFORMS and BetterBench items and keeps only the materials-specific parts (measured-vs-simulated labelling; a noise ladder built from repeat measurements).

scorecard.principle: Read the rows; keep hand-picked sets apart
scorecard.evidence: plan/plan.md:30 every differing row listed with both formula strings side by side. plan/plan.md:78 'disagrees with the draft key, not wrong'. plan/plan.md:88 seen/unseen breakdown printed beside the headline. plan/plan.md:110 accuracy by band plus a per-scan flag 'were all true ingredients in the candidate list?'. page/big-picture.html:474 calls the pairs file 'a unit-test file for a metric'.
scorecard.gap: Only a wording risk later: 8 of 18 and 13 of 18 come from pairs chosen to be hard and must never be quoted as error rates.
scorecard.fix: In N1 and N5 use CheckList's vocabulary (Ribeiro et al. 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04118, abstract opened this run): the Nb2O5 vs Nb12O29 row is a minimum-functionality test, the mirror-image row is an invariance test. Report 'unit tests failed', never 'percent wrong'.

scorecard.principle: Replicate before you generalise
scorecard.evidence: plan/plan.md:151 'Selling the 12-to-32 swing as a field-wide finding' is on the don't list. plan/plan.md:165 (correction 2) scopes the claim to 'the 40 weighed scans in your local set-up'. page/big-picture.html:429 'A pattern in our own measurements, not a field-wide fact'. plan/plan.md:185 scopes the TE floor to 3,593 of 12,222 rows and formula-only models.
scorecard.gap: The natural replication is implied but not written: N3 does not say its results get re-marked under every rule.
scorecard.fix: Add one line to N3: 'Re-mark N3's results under every rule with the N1 runner; this is the second-dataset test of the marking effect'.

scorecard.principle: Assume the score will be gamed
scorecard.evidence: Follows on the user's own project: plan/plan.md:104 any change needs 'a dated amendment to the frozen plan, with old and new numbers side by side'. plan/plan.md:79 and :104 allow 'cannot tell' and 'specialists disagree' tiers but give them no score. Nothing in the plan says how per-phase tiers roll up into a per-scan mark or whether extra wrong phases are charged. synth/gaps.md:232: 'adding a spurious phase always improves the match'. Web, opened this run: the Dara paper's rule excludes spurious phases; RADAR-PD's any-match rule does not charge for extras.
scorecard.gap: Under an any-match rule a tool that lists more phases gains. 'Cannot tell' becomes a free pass if it counts as correct or drops out of the denominator. The lenient rule already merges different compounds (plan/plan.md:79).
scorecard.fix: D1 table: four count columns per scan (true phases, predicted phases, missed, extra). N1 spec: report missed and extra separately as well as exact-set; 'cannot tell' is its own reported share and never counts as correct; two unit tests must pass under every preset: padding the answer with a wrong phase does not raise the score, and a vaguer formula does not raise the score.
scorecard.effort: 15 minutes at D1; about a day inside N1

scorecard.principle: No user, no benchmark
scorecard.evidence: plan/plan.md:23 'It has a sure first user: your own project'. plan/plan.md:62-65 'The one question only you can answer'. plan/plan.md:104 'Check whether the installed Dara package already ships the paper's own marking script; if so, it is the natural sixth rule' and 'Ship a CSV plus one Python file, not a package or a site'. plan/plan.md:171 (correction 8): 'No installable grader exists' rests on one unchecked checker.
scorecard.gap: plan/plan.md:36 lets a residual count alone decide 'reusable marker is worth building'. A marking problem can be real and a reusable kit still go unused. No outside user is named; the plan admits this.
scorecard.fix: Split the D1 verdict into two lines. Line 1, from the count: 'the marking problem is real / not real on this set'. Line 2: 'build for others only if one named outside tool author, benchmark host or specialist says they would run it; otherwise build for my project only'. When the time comes, prefer offering the rules plus the signature as an option inside an existing script over a new standalone. No contact without the user's yes.
scorecard.effort: 5 minutes; fold into the P2 protocol

direction_findings.claim: The order is right: test the scoring rule before building on it. The plan is fine here.
direction_findings.evidence: plan/plan.md:19-25 starts with a 1-2 day test, not a build, and every outcome is cheap. This matches how metric problems were handled in ML: sacreBLEU (Post 2018, opened this run) began from showing the same metric moved by up to 1.8 points across configurations; CheckList (opened this run) showed unit-test style files find failures that aggregate accuracy hides. The plan also already used headroom to kill two ideas (plan/plan.md:146, :91) and words claims locally (plan/plan.md:151).
direction_findings.recommendation: Keep the order. Do not add more pre-work than the three must-fix items below.

direction_findings.claim: The first step's verdict is under-specified in three ways that cannot be repaired afterwards: no threshold, undefined bins, and a judge with a stake.
direction_findings.evidence: plan/plan.md:30 (two undefined bins), :36 (one-line verdict, no rule), :23 (the sorter's own pilot goes 0.309 to 0.745 with the rule), :79 (plan itself says formula-only judging needs 'cannot tell', but the sort has no such bin). The 12, 17 and 32 are already known, so the only new number is the hand-sort count, and 40 rows on 20 powders can only separate 'almost none' from 'many' (my arithmetic, see P4).
direction_findings.recommendation: Write and hash a half-page protocol first: three defined bins, a three-way rule with a grey zone, counts in powders, two blind sorting passes, and a verdict split into 'problem real on this set?' and 'build for others?' (the second needs a named outside user). About 2-3 hours in total.

direction_findings.claim: The field scores X-ray phase naming in at least three non-comparable units today. That makes a signature-first marker the smallest adoptable contribution, ahead of a new tier vocabulary.
direction_findings.evidence: Opened this run: the Dara paper counts a scan correct only if all added ingredients are found and no spurious ones are listed (arxiv.org/html/2510.19667). RADAR-PD counts a sample correct if any predicted candidate matches any reference label, as judged by a GPT-4 prompt, with no reported check against people (arxiv.org/html/2605.12478). GALAXI, 7 September 2026, reports micro-F1 0.935 and its abstract gives no matching rule or test size (arxiv.org/abs/2609.06908). One web search in this run found no standard scoring tool for this task; that is a negative search, not proof. plan/plan.md:164 shows the user's own spread has the same anatomy (rule, stale marks, library).
direction_findings.recommendation: If D1 says 'real', make N1's first deliverable the settings string plus a runner that re-marks one results file under the field's existing rules (exact set with no spurious phases; any-match; formula strict; formula lenient). Tiers come second. 'Print your settings' is easier for others to adopt than 'adopt my tiers'.

direction_findings.claim: Most desk items are local replications of known evaluation practice. That is fine for learning and for the user's own project, but novelty claims must shrink. Only two items are open from this lens, and the plan's X-ray lean matches them.
direction_findings.evidence: D4 = standard statistics (Miller 2024; McNemar). N2's general point is 8 years old in materials (Meredig et al. 2018) and general in science (Kapoor and Narayanan 2022); a 2026 TE paper reportedly already shows a composition-wise split drop (search snippet only, never opened). N4 has a close cousin with a released package (Crusius et al. 2025, never opened). N5 overlaps REFORMS and BetterBench. All of these were opened or searched by stage 1, not by me. Open items: (a) a versioned X-ray marker checked against more than one specialist; (b) a hidden, machine-scored weighed-mixture exam with governance. plan/plan.md:57 already cashes TE in as 'a short note plus one frozen test list', which is the right size.
direction_findings.recommendation: Keep the plan's sizes. Add citations and the words 'local replication of a known effect' to N2, N4, N5 and D4. Let N5 claim only the materials-specific parts: measured-vs-simulated labelling and a noise ladder built from repeat measurements.

direction_findings.claim: A weighed-mixture exam has certain answers but may measure a narrow skill. The plan's own numbers show the two sample types behave in opposite ways.
direction_findings.evidence: plan/plan.md:165: on 40 weighed scans tools tie and the rule matters a lot; on 20 reaction products the rule moves 1-3 of 20 and tools differ by 11-13. plan/plan.md:198 (correction 29) admits 'one lab is enough' is reasoning, not fact. The Reynolds Cup (synth/gaps.md:209) is already a blind weighed-mixture contest for human analysts scored on amounts, so L2's new part is only 'standing, machine-scored, naming'. Whether accuracy on weighed mixtures predicts accuracy on real reaction products is unknown, and it cannot be tested at the desk with one local tool.
direction_findings.recommendation: Say this limit in the L2 one-pager next to 'one-instrument exam'. Treat N3 as the go/no-go for L2: proceed only if the hard bands show real headroom (P8) and the marking effect replicates when N3 is re-marked (P12). Accept that the honest outcome may be 'out of our reach', as the plan already says.

direction_findings.claim: This is evaluation work by an explicit early decision, not by drift. But the user's stated aim is data curation, and only L2 creates new data.
direction_findings.evidence: synth/storyline.md:63 'Decision: evaluation data before a training corpus'. synth/glossary_usermodel.md (Goals section) quotes the user on 'collecting, curating, recovering, connecting' experimental evidence. In plan.md, D1-D6 and N1-N6 audit or re-score existing data; L2 (plan/plan.md:127) is the only item that makes new test items, and it needs a lab.
direction_findings.recommendation: No change to the plan. Say it plainly to the user at the week-2 sitting: 'until L2 you are auditing exams, not making one'. If that does not match their aim, the fork question (plan/plan.md:62) is where to change course.

top_changes: Before opening the project folders, write and hash a half-page protocol for the 40-row test: three sorting bins with written definitions and worked examples (add 'cannot tell from formula alone'), a three-way decision rule with a grey zone fixed in advance, counts stated in powders (20) as well as scans (40), and the verdict split into two lines: 'problem real on this set?' (from the count) and 'build for others?' (only with one named outside user). This cannot be repaired after the rows are seen.

Sort the differing rows in two blind passes, report how often they agree, and label the verdict 'draft, not specialist-reviewed'. The rows where the passes differ become the first rows for a specialist. Copy the page's '10 unseen pairs' held-out check into plan.md L1.

Add a settings string to every mark in the 40-row table (rule and code hash, tolerance, formula clean-up version, Dara version, reference library and snapshot, candidate cap, scan-level meaning of 'correct', date) and four count columns (true, predicted, missed, extra phases). Extend the done-test: each of 12, 17, 32 and 38 is explained by naming which fields differ. This is the sacreBLEU idea and the real diagnostic for correction 1.

Fix the statistics and splits before the second week: the 'tie or not?' function takes a cluster ID and a paired flag (20 powders, papers); the TE leak report prints two keys (paper and formula); N2 gets a dev set cut from the training papers, with neighbour count and tree settings chosen on dev only and 1-neighbour reported beside 5-neighbour.

Shrink and cite. D4, N2, N4 and N5 are local replications or specialisations of known work (Miller 2024; Meredig 2018; Kapoor and Narayanan 2022; Crusius 2025; REFORMS; BetterBench): say so. If D1 says 'real', make N1 signature-first and include the field's existing rules (exact set with no spurious phases; any-match). Add a floor and ceiling per band to N3, make N3 the go/no-go for L2, and add five governance lines to the L2 draft (custodian does not enter, hashed key, submission cap, fresh powders each round, scrubbed file names and headers).
audit.verdict_on_proceeding: Proceed with changes. The direction is sound from an evaluation-science view and 2 of 14 principles already pass fully (11 partly, none violated outright), but three cheap fixes (pre-written decision rule and bin definitions, two blind sorting passes, a settings string on every mark; about 2-3 hours together) must go in before the 40-row test because they cannot be added honestly after the rows have been seen; everything else can wait until the item it belongs to.

verdicts.target: is_eval_work: 'mostly' ... 'Meta-evaluation for materials ML on measured data: auditing how the exams are set, marked and sized'
verdicts.why: The split into eval items (D1, D3, D4, D6, N1-N5, L1, L2, L5) and non-eval items (D0, D5, L3, L4, N6, most of D2) is right, and correction 12 (plan.md:177) is quoted correctly. Two corrections. (1) 'Explicit early decision' overstates it: storyline.md:63 tags that line [OPINION, arithmetic] and adds 'Which track goes first was never decided'. It was a session conclusion the user went along with. (2) The audit sets eval against the user's aim of data curation. The user's own anchor quote (glossary_usermodel.md:258) lists missing 'clearly defined problems and evaluation metrics' as part of the data problem. So eval work sits inside the stated aim. Also: until it replicates elsewhere, D1 is closer to debugging one project's grader than to evaluation research.
verdicts.corrected_text: Yes, mostly. About two thirds of the plan is evaluation work, and most of that is meta-evaluation: checking how existing exams are marked, split and sized. The rest is data-error reporting and file housekeeping. This came from a session recommendation (storyline.md:63), not from a stated user decision, but it matches a gap the user's own anchor quote names: measured datasets lack clearly defined problems and evaluation metrics. Only L2 makes new test data, and L2 needs a lab. D1 starts as a bug hunt in one grader; it becomes evaluation research only if the effect shows up on a second dataset.

verdicts.target: P1 Split by the unit that leaks: 'The leak report names one sibling key ... one key cannot explain the number'
verdicts.why: Half of this is already in the plan. D3 (plan.md:88) prints the seen/unseen breakdown beside the headline: 3,593 of 12,222 test rows have a same-formula sibling in training. That IS the second key. Adding it to the 30-line report is a formatting change, not a fix. The powder point is the real catch and the evidence is real: gaps.md:208 confirms 20 powders each scanned for 2 and 8 minutes, and builds.md:354 says only exact duplicates straddling the split were flagged as unchecked. A 2-minute and 8-minute scan of one powder are not byte-duplicates, so D2's hash check would miss them. Not must-fix: agreed. Meredig 2018 and Kapoor and Narayanan exist (search listings only; the journal version of the latter is 2023, preprint 2022).
verdicts.corrected_text: D2's private check groups by powder (mixture ID parsed from the file name), not only by file hash: are the 2-minute and 8-minute scans of one powder on the same side of the calibration/test split? Report yes/no; change nothing. D3's leak report prints both keys it already computes: same-paper sibling share (must be 0 on the paper split) and same-formula sibling share (3,593 of 12,222).

verdicts.target: P2 Freeze test list and decision rule first: 'write a dated half-page protocol and hash it ... This is the one thing that cannot be repaired after the rows have been seen'
verdicts.why: The most important row, and the gap is real: plan.md:30 has two undefined bins, plan.md:36 has a verdict with no rule, plan.md:79 says formula-only judging needs 'cannot tell'. Three corrections. (a) The rows are not unseen. gaps.md:153 records an earlier session's recount of these same 40 scans and its reading: 'The misses are naming artifacts', with three examples (LaO3, Ni1.875O2, V4O9.93316). The audit even proposes those rows as worked examples. So this is a decision rule written before a recount, not a blind pre-registration, and the likely answer already leans 'spelling'. Say that. (b) Wrong unit. The thresholds '2 or fewer of 40 / 8 or more of 40' count rows. The 40 scans are 20 powders mixed from a short closed list of bought ingredients (gaps.md:208 lists 10 single-ingredient scans, so roughly 10 ingredients; my inference). One artifact such as LaO3 for La(OH)3 repeats in every scan that contains that ingredient. Count DISTINCT (true formula, program formula) pairs. Expect roughly 5 to 15. (c) Hashing a private half-page is ceremony. D0 already writes content hashes for the rescue folder; a dated text file there is enough. The N2 dev-split advice is standard and correctly placed later.
verdicts.corrected_text: Before the working session opens the project folders, write one dated page in the rescue folder: (1) three bins with definitions: spelling artifact (same compound, different string), real chemistry disagreement (different compound), cannot tell from formula alone; (2) the unit is distinct formula pairs, with row and powder counts shown beside; (3) a three-way rule on distinct pairs, numbers chosen by the user, with a middle zone that means 'undecided, look at the pilot rows and N3'; (4) one sentence admitting an earlier session already read these rows as naming artifacts. About one hour. No hash ritual.

verdicts.target: P3 Intervals that respect clusters; compare paired: 'tie_or_not(scores_a, scores_b=None, cluster_id=None, paired=True) ... three tests'
verdicts.why: Evidence is real (plan.md:90-91; page line 499; builds.md:702 'count clusters'). Partly already handled: the test interval in D4 (0.0 to 15.0) is the PAIRED interval from gaps.md:207, so pairing is implicit in the plan. Clustering is the real add and costs an hour. Miller 2024 checked in the body this run: section 2.2 covers clustered questions, 4.2 paired differences, 5 power. Refuted part: the second proposed test, a paired significance test of strict vs lenient on the 18 tricky pairs. Those pairs were hand-picked to be hard. A p-value on them contradicts the audit's own P11 ('never quote hand-picked sets as rates'). The arithmetic (p = 0.0625 at best) is right but the test is meaningless. With 20 clusters a bootstrap is rough, so the function needs a third output.
verdicts.corrected_text: tie_or_not takes a cluster ID and a paired flag and returns one of three words: 'not a tie', 'tie', 'too small to tell'. Two tests: 38 vs 35 of 40 resampled over 20 powders returns 'tie'; one thermoelectric case resampled over papers. No significance test on the hand-built tricky pairs. Cite Miller 2024 sections 2.2 and 4.2. Claim no novelty.

verdicts.target: P4 Size the test before building it: '40 rows on 20 powders cannot fix prevalence to better than about plus or minus 10 points'
verdicts.why: The arithmetic is right (I get a Wilson interval of about 5.5% to 26% for 5 of 40). The framing is wrong. D1 is a full count of one small benchmark, not a sample from a population. No interval lets it speak for other data, and the plan already bans that claim (plan.md:151). The honest sizing statement is about distinct pairs and scope, not plus or minus 10 points. The audit's 'optional' second sheet should be promoted: the 18 rule-dependent rows among the 210 pilot rows (gaps.md:153) come from more varied samples and are on the same disk under the same read-only yes. First check whether those pilot rows overlap the 40 scans (the n=55 pilot and the 56-row stale file may be the same scans; the notes do not say).
verdicts.corrected_text: D1 protocol sentence: 'This is a full count on one 20-powder benchmark built from about 10 ingredients. It measures nothing about other datasets.' D1 gains a second sheet: hand-sort the 18 rule-dependent pilot rows with the same bins, after checking they are not the same 40 scans. After D6, write each band's powder count and the interval it gives before asking for any download (keep as the audit says).

verdicts.target: P5 Give the metric a signature and version: 'Add one signature string per mark to the 40-row table ... must_fix_before_first_step: true'
verdicts.why: The best web-backed row. Verified this run: the Dara paper marks a scan correct only if it 'includes all precursor phases ... and excludes any spurious phases', and reports 18/20 plus 20/20 = 38 of 40. RADAR-PD counts a sample correct if any returned candidate matches, judged by a GPT-4 prompt, n = 291. GALAXI's abstract gives micro-F1 0.935 with no rule or test size. Dara version 1.1.12 and the cap of 80 are in gaps.md:213, not invented. Four corrections. (a) It is not a precondition. These are columns filled while the table is built; nothing is lost if they are added on day 2. Part of D1, not a gate before it. (b) For the two 'as stored' marks most fields will be unknown. Write 'unknown'; that is the finding. (c) 'Each of 12, 17, 32 and 38 is explained' is too strong for 38. The user cannot re-run the paper's set-up. Also, the fetch summary of the Dara paper did not find a statement of which reference library the mixture benchmark used, so 'the paper used the paid library' (gaps.md:153) is unverified by me. Attribute, do not claim to explain. (d) The field that matters most is missing from the plan entirely: what makes a whole SCAN correct. If the user's marker is looser or stricter than 'all true phases and no extras', that is a fourth cause of the spread.
verdicts.corrected_text: First line of D1: write down what makes a scan correct in the user's marker and in the Dara paper (all true phases found and no extra ones). Then add signature columns while building the table: rule and code hash, tolerance, formula clean-up version, Dara version, reference library and date, candidate cap, scan-level rule, date computed. Stored marks get 'unknown' where the field was never saved. Done-test wording: '12, 17 and 32 are explained by named fields; 38 is attributed to named differences, not reproduced'.

verdicts.target: P6 Check the metric against expert judgment: 'two blind passes over the differing rows (for example two separate AI sessions ...) Report raw agreement ... must_fix_before_first_step: true'
verdicts.why: The gap is real: the hand-sort is a labelling task with one interested rater. The fix is weak. Two sessions of the same model are not independent raters; their agreement measures sampling noise. On about 10 distinct pairs an agreement figure is not a statistic. The audit faults RADAR-PD for an LLM judge with no check against people, then prescribes the same thing. A cheaper and more honest second pass uses different EVIDENCE, not a second opinion: for each distinct pair, look up whether the program's odd formula is a known entry of the same structure in the open reference library (for example a nickel-poor entry filed under the NiO structure, or a hydroxide whose hydrogen was never located). Record 'source checked: yes/no' per pair. The user reads the bins and owns the verdict. Not a gate before D1; it is how the sort is done. Keeping the label 'draft, not specialist-reviewed' is right. The '10 unseen pairs' line is already on the page the user reads (page line 614); copying it into plan.md is tidy, not material.
verdicts.corrected_text: D1 sort: one pass by the working session using the written bins; for every distinct pair a lookup column says what the reference entry behind the program's formula actually is, or 'not found'. The user reviews the pairs marked 'cannot tell' and 'real chemistry'. Verdict labelled 'draft, not specialist-reviewed'. These pairs are the first rows shown to a specialist at L1. No agreement percentage is reported.

verdicts.target: P7 Say what decision the score supports: 'append to the D1 verdict line on weighed mixtures in my set-up; on 20 reaction products the rule moved 1-3 of 20'
verdicts.why: The one-line scope note is fine but the user already sees it (page lines 423-424, correction 2). The audit stops short of the real construct problem. D1 on the 40 weighed scans can reveal only ONE failure direction: strict marking rejecting a right answer because of spelling. The other direction, lenient marking accepting a wrong compound (Nb2O5 vs Nb12O29, gaps.md:153), comes from the hand-built tricky pairs. Bought ingredients from a short known list will rarely produce such near-miss compounds. So a 'bug-fix' verdict on the 40 would NOT show the lenient rule is safe on reaction products or open collections, which is where the user's project also runs (builds.md:351).
verdicts.corrected_text: D1 verdict line carries two scope notes: 'on 40 weighed scans in my set-up' and 'this test can show strict-too-strict only; it cannot show lenient-too-loose'. The second direction is tested on the pilot rows (second sheet) and later on N3. Per-preset 'user / decision / tiers that count' lines wait for N1, as the audit says.

verdicts.target: P8 Show floor, ceiling and headroom: 'L2's sizing rests on an unconfirmed 50%'
verdicts.why: Adding a trivial floor and a ceiling line per band to N3 is good and cheap, and making N3 the go/no-go for L2 is sound. But the quoted gap is wrong. 385 is the worst case: 1.96 squared times 0.25 divided by 0.05 squared. If accuracy is far from 50%, FEWER powders give the same interval. The plan's sizing is conservative, not fragile. The real risk is headroom: if tools score near 100% on the hard bands, no sample size separates them. The audit's go/no-go already covers that. The detection-limit figure (1 to 5% by weight) is unverified by anyone. Crusius et al. 2025 exists (Faraday Discussions 256, 304-321, search listing); the page returned 403, so 'ships a package' is unverified.
verdicts.corrected_text: N3 table adds per band: a trivial floor (name only the major ingredients), Dara's score, and a ceiling note marked 'unverified' until a source is opened. L2 request is sent only if hard-band accuracy is clearly below 100% and above the floor. Drop the sentence about 50%; the 385 figure is already the worst case.

verdicts.target: P9 A hidden test needs rules, not just secrecy: 'Add five lines to the L2 draft'
verdicts.why: Correct in principle, months away, and it changes nothing this month. Three of the five lines earn their place. File-name scrubbing is confirmed: the Dara repository README gives the naming pattern precursor1_wt1-precursor2_wt2--2min.xrdml, so recipes sit in file names. Instrument file headers carry sample names too. A submission cap and a refresh schedule are answers to a problem the user would be lucky to have: gaps.md:330 records a metal-printing benchmark with 3 submissions against 6,044 downloads. Missed by the audit: the user is a tool author (dara-conform scores phase identification). 'Custodian does not enter' therefore means the LAB holds the key, or the user's tool is shown as an organiser entry and not ranked.
verdicts.corrected_text: L2 draft gains three lines now: the partner lab (not the user) holds the answer key and lodges its hash before release; file names and file headers carry a random ID only; the user's own tool is listed as an organiser entry, unranked. Submission caps and refresh rounds are noted as 'decide if a second entrant appears'.

verdicts.target: P10 Ship a datasheet with every artefact: 'One 8-field header pasted on top of every CSV from D1 onward'
verdicts.why: Eight fields on every private working file is process for its own sake. The measured problem in this project is too little shipped (plan.md:143: 3 of 188 action items had all four basics), not too little paperwork. Apply a short header only to files that may leave the desk. 'Metric signature' duplicates P5. The N5 mapping is worth keeping: REFORMS has 32 questions and BetterBench 46 practices across 24 benchmarks (both abstracts opened this run), so N5 would otherwise restate them.
verdicts.corrected_text: A 5-field header (source snapshot and hash; how rows were chosen; who or what made the labels; licence; not-for uses) on three files only: the tricky-pairs CSV, the frozen paper-ID list, the match table. N5 starts with one hour mapping its four questions onto REFORMS and BetterBench and keeps only what they lack: measured-vs-simulated labelling and a noise ladder from repeat measurements.

verdicts.target: P13 Assume the score will be gamed: 'four count columns per scan ... two unit tests must pass under every preset'
verdicts.why: The four count columns (true, predicted, missed, extra phases) are the best cheap add in the audit: 15 minutes, and they make the scan-level rule visible. Verified: RADAR-PD scores ALL returned candidates, no fixed list length, no charge for extras. Nuance the audit lacks: that benchmark is single-phase minerals, so its rule is closer to unlimited top-k retrieval than to a multiphase marking rule. 'A vaguer formula does not raise the score' is not testable as written. Note the user's own project added a hydrogen rule that lifted pilot accuracy from 0.545 to 0.745 (gaps.md:153), and the lenient rule merges a hydroxide with a peroxide, so the concrete guard is about hydrogen. Domain precedent the audit missed: the Reynolds Cup (clays.org page opened) scores the sum of absolute weight errors, and misidentified minerals count toward it. Dara reports weight fractions (gaps.md:207), so a weight-error column is possible on weighed mixtures and charges for extras naturally.
verdicts.corrected_text: D1 table: four count columns per scan. N1 later: report missed and extra separately; 'cannot tell' is its own share and never counts as correct; two guard tests: adding a wrong phase never raises the score; a pair that differs only by hydrogen but is a different compound (a hydroxide vs the plain oxide) never returns 'same'. Consider a Reynolds-Cup-style weight-error score as one preset on weighed mixtures.

verdicts.target: P14 No user, no benchmark: 'Split the D1 verdict into two lines'
verdicts.why: plan.md:36 does let a count alone decide 'reusable marker is worth building', and a problem can be real while a kit goes unused. Two lines cost five minutes. One trim: line 2 is the plan's existing fork question (plan.md:62, willing to approach one specialist) restated. Say so instead of adding a new gate. The Dara repository listing shows run scripts (run_precursor_mixture.py) but no scoring script at directory level, which weakly supports 'no shipped marker'; a directory listing is not proof.

verdicts.target: Direction 1: 'The order is right: test the scoring rule before building on it'
verdicts.why: plan.md:19-25 is a test, not a build, and both outcomes are cheap. Post 2018 verified (differences as high as 1.8 between common configurations). Nothing to change.

verdicts.target: Direction 2: 'The first step's verdict is under-specified in three ways that cannot be repaired afterwards' (severity high)
verdicts.why: Under-specified: yes. 'Cannot be repaired afterwards' and 'high' overstate it. An earlier session already read these rows and called the misses naming artifacts (gaps.md:153). The decision is private and reversible: a wrong 'worth building' costs 2-3 weeks of N1, which is itself gated by a specialist check before publishing (plan.md:125). The unit is wrong in the proposed rule (rows, not distinct pairs). Severity medium. Fix is one hour, not 2-3.
verdicts.corrected_text: Medium. Write the bins, the unit (distinct formula pairs) and a three-way rule on one dated page before the recount. Admit on that page that a prior session already leaned 'naming artifacts'. Split the verdict into 'real on this set?' and 'build for others?'.

verdicts.target: Direction 3: 'The field scores X-ray phase naming in at least three non-comparable units today ... signature-first marker is the smallest adoptable contribution'
verdicts.why: All three papers verified this run and say what is claimed. Nuance: they are partly three different TASKS, not three rules for one task. Dara: multiphase weighed mixtures, exact set, no extras. RADAR-PD: 291 single-phase minerals, any returned candidate may match, LLM judge. GALAXI: per-phase micro-F1, rule not in the abstract. A settings string still helps, but it will not make these numbers comparable. 'Easier for others to adopt' is opinion with no evidence. It stays conditional on D1.
verdicts.corrected_text: Three 2025-2026 papers report phase-naming accuracy under three different rules on three different kinds of sample. No shared marking tool turned up in two shallow searches. If D1 and the pilot rows say the problem is real, N1 starts with a settings string and a runner that re-marks one results file under exact-set-no-extras, any-match, formula strict and formula lenient. Tiers second.

verdicts.target: Direction 4: 'Most desk items are local replications of known evaluation practice ... novelty claims must shrink'
verdicts.why: Right, and stronger than stated for N2. A 2026 Materials and Design paper (search snippet only; page 403) reports thermoelectric R-squared near 0.96 on a random split falling to 0.82-0.88 when whole compositions are held out. The plan's own correction 17 says unseen formulas drive most of the 25.5-to-42.2 jump. So the main N2 effect is already published for this property family. What is left is the smaller paper-held-out effect on seen formulas (24.8% to 29.4%), the sign-flip reporting, and the frozen list. plan.md:107 already says 'if an audit exists, shrink'. Apply it. Meredig 2018 (leave-one-cluster-out) and Kapoor and Narayanan (journal year 2023) are real per search listings.

verdicts.target: Direction 5: 'A weighed-mixture exam has certain answers but may measure a narrow skill'
verdicts.why: plan.md:165 and :198 are quoted correctly. Reynolds Cup verified on its own page: held every two years since 2002, blind weighed mineral mixtures, human labs, scored by sum of absolute weight errors. So L2's new part is only 'standing, machine-scored, naming-focused'. Whether weighed-mixture accuracy predicts reaction-product accuracy is unknown and not testable at the desk with one tool. Making N3 the go/no-go is proportionate.

verdicts.target: Direction 6: 'This is evaluation work by an explicit early decision, not by drift. But the user's stated aim is data curation, and only L2 creates new data'
verdicts.why: See is_eval_work. storyline.md:63 is an [OPINION] session conclusion, and the track order 'was never decided'. The user's anchor quote puts evaluation metrics inside the data problem, so the tension is smaller than stated. 'Only L2 creates new test data' is correct and worth saying plainly.
verdicts.corrected_text: Until L2 the work audits exams; it does not make one. That fits the user's stated gap (no clear problems or evaluation metrics for measured data) but not the 'collecting and curating' half of it. Raise this at the week-2 sitting, at the fork question.

verdicts.target: Top change 1: 'Before opening the project folders, write and hash a half-page protocol ...'
verdicts.why: Keep; trim. Drop the hash. Change the unit to distinct formula pairs. Add the admission that the rows were already read once. Add the scan-level meaning of 'correct' as the first line.
verdicts.corrected_text: One dated page, one hour, before the recount: what makes a scan correct; three bins with definitions and examples; unit = distinct (true, program) formula pairs with rows and powders shown beside; a three-way rule with a middle zone; verdict in two lines; a note that an earlier session already read the misses as naming artifacts.

verdicts.target: Top change 2: 'Sort the differing rows in two blind passes, report how often they agree'
verdicts.why: Two runs of one model are not two raters, and agreement on about 10 pairs is noise. Replace opinion-vs-opinion with a source lookup per pair.
verdicts.corrected_text: One sorting pass plus a lookup column per distinct pair (what reference entry sits behind the program's formula). User reviews the non-spelling pairs. Verdict labelled 'draft, not specialist-reviewed'. Those pairs go first to a specialist.

verdicts.target: Top change 3: 'Add a settings string to every mark ... and four count columns ... Extend the done-test'
verdicts.why: Sound and cheap, but it is work inside D1, not a gate before it. Stored marks will have unknown fields. '38 is explained' must become '38 is attributed'.
verdicts.corrected_text: Inside D1: settings columns (unknown where never saved) and four count columns. Done-test: 12, 17, 32 explained by named fields; 38 attributed, not reproduced.

verdicts.target: Top change 4: 'Fix the statistics and splits before the second week'
verdicts.why: Cluster ID and paired flag, a dev split cut from training papers, 1-neighbour beside 5-neighbour: all standard, about half a day plus an hour, correctly timed. Only trims: the formula key is already printed by D3, and the significance test on hand-picked tricky pairs should be dropped.

verdicts.target: Top change 5: 'Shrink and cite ... N3 floor and ceiling, N3 as go/no-go for L2, five governance lines'
verdicts.why: Shrink-and-cite holds and N2 should shrink further (composition-split result already published for thermoelectrics, per snippet). Fix the wrong remark about 50%. Cut governance to three lines and add the missed conflict: the user is a tool author.
verdicts.corrected_text: Label D4, N2, N4, N5 'local replication of a known effect' with citations. N2 shrinks to the seen-formula paper effect, sign accuracy and the frozen list unless the 1-2 hour search finds nothing. N3 gets floor and ceiling per band and gates L2. L2 draft: lab holds the key and lodges a hash; random-ID file names and headers; user's tool unranked.

verdicts.target: verdict_on_proceeding: 'Proceed with changes ... 2 of 14 principles already pass fully (11 partly) ... three cheap fixes (about 2-3 hours) must go in before the 40-row test'
verdicts.why: Proceed: yes. Arithmetic slip: the scorecard has 12 'partly' and 2 'follows', not 11. A card that is 12 of 14 'partly' barely discriminates; only P2, P5 and P13's count columns change what happens this week, and P3 next week. Of the three 'must-fix before' items only the written rule is a true precondition. The settings columns and the sorting method are part of doing D1.
verdicts.corrected_text: Proceed. One precondition: a one-hour dated page (scan-level rule, bins, unit, three-way rule, two-line verdict). Two things folded into D1 itself: settings and count columns; a lookup column instead of a second opinion. Everything else waits for its own item. This should be the last check before D1 starts.

citation_checks.note: Opened root, /scripts and /dataset listings this run. Scripts include run_precursor_mixture.py but nothing named as a scoring or marking script (a listing is not proof). Dataset README says mixtures are 'equal weight' and gives the file-name pattern precursor1_wt1-precursor2_wt2[-precursor3_wt3]--[2min|8min].xrdml, confirming that recipes sit in file names (gaps.md:210) and that the README wording conflicts with 10-90 wt% mixtures (gaps.md:109).

missed: The 40 rows have already been read once. gaps.md:153 records an earlier session's recount and its conclusion: 'The misses are naming artifacts' (three examples given). D1's likely answer is therefore foreshadowed. The audit treats D1 as unseen data and builds a pre-registration on that. Honest wording: a decision rule written before a RECOUNT.

Wrong counting unit. The 40 scans are 20 powders mixed from a short closed list of bought ingredients (10 single-ingredient scans per gaps.md:208; about 10 ingredients is my inference). One naming artifact repeats in every scan containing that ingredient. Any threshold must count distinct (true formula, program formula) pairs, probably 5 to 15, not rows out of 40.

D1 can only detect one of the two failure directions. Weighed mixtures of known ingredients can show 'strict marking rejects a right answer'. They will rarely show 'lenient marking accepts a wrong compound' (the Nb2O5 vs Nb12O29 kind), which comes from hand-built pairs. The 18 rule-dependent rows among the 210 pilot rows (gaps.md:153) are on the same disk and cover more varied samples. They should be part of D1, not optional.

The user's metric was already tuned once on the data it scores. gaps.md:153: pilot accuracy moved from 0.545 to 0.745 'after one rule about hydrogen was added'. The project was pre-registered on 2026-07-09 (builds.md:351). Whether the hydrogen rule came before or after that freeze is not in the notes. First-hour check; if after, it needs the dated amendment the plan already requires (plan.md:104).

Possible double counting of evidence. The plan's reason 2 for D1 (0.309 vs 0.745, n = 55) and the 56-row stale results file may be the same Dara benchmark scans as the 12/17/32 of 40. The notes do not say. If they overlap, 'a sure first user' is not independent evidence that the rule matters. Check in the first hour.

Conflict of interest at L2. The user authors a tool (dara-conform) that would sit the exam the user would organise. The audit writes 'custodian does not enter' without noticing the custodian is a contestant. The partner lab should hold the key, or the user's tool is shown unranked.

A domain-native scoring precedent exists. The Reynolds Cup scores the sum of absolute weight errors and charges for misidentified minerals (page opened this run). Dara reports weight fractions (gaps.md:207: error 4.81 vs 5.49). On weighed mixtures a weight-error score penalises extra phases naturally and sidesteps part of the formula-string problem. N1 should include it as one preset before inventing tiers.

Known errors in the benchmark's own documentation belong in D1's notes: the Dara dataset README says 'equal weight' (confirmed on the repository page) while the notes say mixtures run 10 to 90 wt% (gaps.md:109), and file names spell out the recipe. Any tool that can read file names, including LLM agents, is contaminated on this set. This matters for N3 as well as L2.

Meta-risk: checking as a substitute for shipping. The project measured its own pattern (plan.md:143: 3 of 188 action items complete; builds.md:702: some pre-registered checks 'passed by construction'). The audit adds 14 rows of fixes. It should say plainly that principle-checking is capped at about one hour before D1 and that this review is the last pre-check.

N2's remaining novelty is thinner than the audit says. If the 2026 composition-split result for thermoelectrics holds up (snippet only), the main effect in the user's note is published. The plan's own rule at plan.md:107 then applies: shrink to the frozen list plus the paper-ID index.

Small slips in the audit itself: it says 11 rows are 'partly' but lists 12; it cites Kapoor and Narayanan as 2022 where the journal version is 2023; it calls L2's 385-powder figure dependent on 'an unconfirmed 50%' when 50% is the worst case.
challenge.overall:
The audit survives, smaller. Its file and line references are real. The seven web sources it leans on most are real and say what it claims (Post 2018, Miller 2024, the Dara paper, RADAR-PD, GALAXI, CheckList; plus REFORMS and BetterBench, which I opened myself). Nothing is refuted outright. Almost every fix needs trimming.

Answer to the user's question: yes, this is mostly evaluation work, and mostly meta-evaluation (testing the tests). Yes, a principles check before starting was worth doing. It should now stop. One hour of writing is the only true precondition for the 40-row test.

What holds and matters this week: (1) write the decision rule and bin definitions before the recount; (2) write down what makes a whole scan 'correct' (the Dara paper requires all true phases and no extra ones; the plan never states the user's rule); (3) add settings columns and missed/extra counts while building the table. Next week: make the 'tie or not?' function cluster-aware.

Where the audit is wrong or overbuilt: it treats the 40 rows as unseen when an earlier session already read them as naming artifacts (gaps.md:153). It counts rows when the honest unit is distinct formula pairs from about 10 ingredients. 'Two blind AI passes with an agreement figure' is process theatre; a source lookup per pair is cheaper and better. Hashing a private page, an 8-field header on every private CSV, submission caps for an exam with no entrants, and a significance test on hand-picked pairs should go. The remark that L2's sizing rests on 'an unconfirmed 50%' is backwards; 50% is the worst case. Two of its three 'must fix before' items are really part of doing D1.

What it missed that could change the plan: the 40 weighed scans can show only one failure direction (strict too strict), so the 18 rule-dependent pilot rows should join D1. The user's metric was already tuned once on pilot data (the hydrogen rule, 0.545 to 0.745); check that against the project's freeze date. The user would be both exam organiser and contestant at L2. The Reynolds Cup already offers a diffraction-community scoring rule that charges for wrong phases. And the thermoelectric note may have less left to say than either the plan or the audit assumes.

Unknowns I could not settle: which reference library the Dara paper used for its 38 of 40; whether the Crusius 2025 paper ships code; whether the 2026 thermoelectric split paper says what its snippet says (both pages returned 403); whether the n = 55 pilot overlaps the 40 scans.

is_eval_work.which_parts_are_eval:
- D1 is a unit-test file for a scoring rule, with a draft answer key. That is metric validation.
- D4 is the statistics of comparisons (tie or not).
- D3 is split design: a leak report and a frozen test list.
- D6 is a survey of candidate test sets.
- N1 implements the metric.
- N3 is a practice exam with bands fixed in advance.
- N4 is the best-achievable-score ladder. Metrology calls this the repeatability to reproducibility ladder.
- N5 is a reader's checklist for leaderboards.
- L1 is an expert review of the answer key.
- L2 is a hidden test set.
- L5 is a thermoelectric lab comparison.
- The first step (the 40-row test) is eval work of the most basic kind. It checks the marker before trusting any mark.

In the older field's words, D1, N1 and L1 set the assessment criteria. D4 is proficiency-test scoring. N3, L2 and L5 design the proficiency test. N4 is a precision study.
is_eval_work.which_parts_are_not:
- D0 (file rescue) is housekeeping.
- D2 (499 files that look simulated but are filed as measured) is a data provenance audit. It touches eval in one place only: whether a duplicate pair sits on both sides of the calibration/test split.
- D5, L3 and L4 (error notes and a neutral notice) are error reporting to dataset owners.
- N6 (thermoelectric suspect list) is data quality flagging.
- The critique of one company's 134-item result is secondary reading of someone else's eval. Only its arithmetic (one standard error of about 4.3 points) is eval method.
- The partner-lab part of L2 (weighing, mixing, scanning, checking purity) is reference-material production. In a real proficiency test most of the organiser's effort goes there, not into scoring code.
is_eval_work.best_one_line_name_for_this_work: Checking the exam before trusting the scores: answer keys, marking rules, splits and error bars for ML on measured materials data. Metrology calls this method validation and proficiency-test design.

scorecard.principle: Say exactly what is being measured
scorecard.evidence:

- plan/plan.md:29 asks for "three formula-level marks per scan". It never says what one mark means: all true phases named, or are extras allowed?

- plan/plan.md:97 (D6) lists the row fields (raw scans, weighed answers, licence, powders, format, size). "What task was this set built for" is not among them.

The IUCr quantification round robin told entrants which phases were present (stage-1 reading of the 1998 letter; the page returned 403 to me). Re-using those scans for naming is a new use of that key, and the card should say so. Without a written mark definition, 12, 17 and 32 of 40 cannot be interpreted.
scorecard.fix:
Put a 6-line task card at the top of the 40-row table:
- Task: name phases only.
- One mark: the stored code's rule, written in words.
- Naming level: formula only.
- The wt% range of the 40 mixes.
- Sample: weighed mixtures, 3 phases or fewer, one instrument, 2- and 8-minute scans.
- Inputs: element list given; local open library capped at 80 candidates; Dara version.

Also add a D6 column: "original task: were phases given to entrants? yes/no".

scorecard.principle: The answer key needs its own check

The notes already saw this failure mode. synth/gaps.md:109 records hydrate formulas that differ between two fields. synth/builds.md:565 records a README saying "equal weight" while the file names encode 10-90 wt%.
scorecard.gap:
- No purity scan of each ingredient.
- No independent check of the mix.
- No uncertainty on any weight fraction.

The Reynolds Cup (page re-opened in this run) requires purity known within 1 wt% and checks its splits by XRD and XRF. A bought chemical with 3% of a second phase really shows that phase, so a correct tool gets marked as a false positive. NIST's alumina standard is about 99% crystalline (stage-1 source), so weighed fraction and crystalline fraction differ by up to a few percent.
scorecard.fix:
- Replace "certain" with "known to within ingredient purity and weighing error" in the glossary, in L2 and on the page.
- Add three asks to the L2 one-pager: a scan of each ingredient lot; one bulk-chemistry check (such as XRF) on a random subset; a stated uncertainty per wt%.
- For the 40 scans, use the 10 single-ingredient scans already on disk (synth/gaps.md:208) as the purity check, if the stored results include them. Flag any ingredient whose own scan shows a second phase.
scorecard.effort: Wording 10 min; purity look 1-2 hours inside the first step; L2 lines 15 min

scorecard.principle: Prove the test items are uniform and stable

scorecard.gap:
- In small hand-mixed powders, a 1 wt% ingredient may be only a few grains in the beam, so its peaks are a lottery (particle statistics).
- Many oxides, hydroxides and carbonates take up water or CO2 from air, so the recipe drifts.

Add two lines to the L2 draft:
- Re-split and re-scan a random 10% and compare against a limit set in advance.
- Record the date mixed and the date scanned, and flag air-sensitive ingredients.

scorecard.evidence:

Correction to the compiled notes: they apply this principle to N4. plan/plan.md:112-113 shows N4 is a thermoelectric label-noise ladder, not an X-ray difficulty axis, so that criticism does not apply to N4.
scorecard.gap:
"Harder" means count, amount and scan time. It leaves out the systematic effects the 1998 round robin built one sample each for:
- Microabsorption: heavy grains shade themselves, so their peaks come out weak.
- Preferred orientation: flat or needle grains lie down, so some peaks are too strong.
- Non-crystalline content: glass gives no sharp peaks at all.

The user's own 40 scans already span a 30-fold absorption contrast.
scorecard.fix: Add per-item tags to the N3 score sheet and the L2 recipe list: absorption contrast, plate- or needle-shaped ingredient, non-crystalline ingredient, poorly crystalline ingredient, scan time. scorecard.principle: Report detection by amount, with a floor

A careful lab study put the detection limit near 0.2 wt% on a copper source, with relative error under 20% only above 1 wt% (stage-1 reading of the 2016 abstract). Routine fast scans are worse. A low score in that band says little about the tool.

- D6 row: add "wt% range" and "scan time".

direction_findings.claim: The first step is the right kind of step, and the plan is fine here. Checking the marker before trusting any mark is what a proficiency-test organiser does before round one.
direction_findings.evidence:
- plan/plan.md:19-43: a 40-row table on data already on disk, a done test, two approvals, and no download or contact.
- The plan already matches older practice in five places: a tie rule (plan.md:91); a "cannot tell" verdict with guard rows (plan.md:79-80); bands fixed in advance and a truth-in-candidate-list flag (plan.md:110); public-answer sets called a practice exam (plan.md:110, 141); L2 labelled a one-instrument exam (plan.md:127).
direction_findings.recommendation:
Keep the step. Add three things before building the table, under an hour of writing in all:
- A task card that defines one mark (P1).
- Per-scan missed and extra counts (P8).
- A pre-written sort rule with five bins and a preset go/no-go number (P9).

Treat the hand-sort as a draft until a specialist sees it.

direction_findings.claim: The long-term aim is narrower than the plan thinks. A machine scored against blind-contest weighed mixtures already exists. A standing, hidden, third-party, naming-first exam on synthesis chemistry with a published marking rule still appears open.

I saw a search snippet only this run; Springer redirected to an authorisation flow, not followed. URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42860-020-00105-6

This fits an ML person's assets better than organising powders. It means contacting people, so it waits for the user's yes.

direction_findings.claim: A diffraction person will not be surprised that formula-string marking is unstable. The contribution that survives is a runnable, tested rule with numbers, not the discovery.
