challenge.lens: Adversarial check of the metrology / proficiency-testing audit. I re-read plan.md in full, checked the audit's quoted lines in plan.md, gaps.md, builds.md, the page, the verify_*.md files and the C16 digest (all inside the scratchpad, read-only). On the web I opened: the Reynolds Cup rules page, the Cambridge Core abstract of Butler and Hillier 2021, the PubMed Central full text of Lutterotti et al. 2019, the Dara paper (arXiv abstract and arXiv HTML), the GALAXI arXiv abstract, the Zenodo record for Leon-Reina 2016, the Cambridge abstract of the 2002 search-match round robin, and the NIST page for SRM 676a. IUCr and Wiley pages returned HTTP 403; Springer redirected to a login flow (not followed); PubMed returned a cookie wall. Nothing was downloaded, signed or submitted. Web pages were read through a summarising fetch tool, so short quotes below should be re-checked against the source before being repeated in public.

verdicts.target: is_eval_work: "mostly" ... "Checking the exam before trusting the scores"
verdicts.why: The split is right. D1, D4, D3, D6, N1, N3, N4, N5, L1, L2 check an exam (metric, key, split, error bars). D0, D2, D5, L3, L4, N6 are housekeeping, provenance and error reporting. Two small notes. (1) D4 is closer to a paired comparison of two methods than to proficiency-test z-scoring; the analogy is loose but harmless. (2) The precise ML name is meta-evaluation: validating the metric and the key, not running the benchmark. The audit's most useful sentence is that the partner-lab half of L2 is reference-material production, not desk eval work. That is correct and it is why L2 is further away than it reads.

verdicts.target: P1 partly: "It never says what one mark means" ... 6-line task card, must fix before first step
verdicts.why: True for plan.md: no line defines a mark. But the definition already exists in two places the audit did not open. (a) The user's frozen pre-registration, as recorded in digests/C16-xrd-session-verification.md:29-31: strict = equal reduced formula; lenient = ignore unlocated hydrogen, same elements within distance 0.04 (two-element compounds) or 0.10, phases matched one-to-one. Stored columns are gt_phases and rank1_phases (C16:243). (b) The Dara paper (arXiv 2510.19667, HTML opened this run): only the top-ranked answer is judged; a scan is correct if it includes all weighed phases and excludes any spurious phase. So the card is a 20-minute copy job plus one look at the marker code, not a design task. The audit also missed one card line: top-ranked answer only.
verdicts.corrected_text: Task card (copy, do not invent): Task = name phases. One mark = per scan, top-ranked answer only (column rank1_phases); strict and lenient rules quoted from the project's frozen pre-registration; confirm in code that one-to-one matching means extras make the scan wrong. Published rule for the 38 of 40 = all weighed phases present and no spurious phase, top answer only. Naming level = formula. Sample = 20 mixtures from 10 ingredients, 3 phases or fewer, 2- and 8-minute scans, one instrument. Inputs = element list given; local open library capped at 80 candidates; Dara 1.1.12.

verdicts.target: P2 violates: "Its right answer is certain" ... use the 10 single-ingredient scans as the purity check, 1-2 hours
verdicts.why: The verdict holds and is stronger than the audit knew. The Dara paper itself reports a real extra phase in one of the 20 mixtures (the 30 NiO / 30 Bi2O3 / 40 Li2CO3 mix shows a bismuth carbonate, put down to reaction with Li2CO3 or air during mixing). The authors chose to leave that phase out of their evaluation. That is an analyst's judgement on the key, on the very 40 scans the first step uses. So "needs no analyst's opinion" (plan.md:9) is already false for this set. The proposed first-step fix is not proportionate, though. An earlier checker (plan/verify_K1_newcomer-skeptic.md:20) already said reading the single-ingredient scans "is not a five-minute job for a newcomer", and gaps.md:208 says 8 of the 10 singles sit on a different measurement grid. The first step reads stored results only; it does not run Dara on singles.
verdicts.corrected_text: Reword "certain" to "known to within ingredient purity, weighing error and any reaction during mixing" (plan.md:9, :127; page lines 618, 623). In the 40-row table add one flag column: "recipe has a documented off-recipe phase" and mark the rows that hold both Bi2O3 and Li2CO3, citing the Dara paper. Leave the purity look at the 10 single scans for L1 (the specialist) or for N1. Keep the three L2 asks (ingredient-lot scan, one chemistry check, stated uncertainty) but write them only when L2 is drafted.

verdicts.target: P3 partly: tie function has no key-error input; "The notes do not say whether the interval resamples 20 powders or 40 scans"
verdicts.why: One sub-claim is refuted. The notes do say it: plan/verify_K4_evidence.md:17 and verify_K1_evidence.md:17 record "10,000 resamples of the 20 mixtures (so the real unit is 20 powders)". The audit searched the verify files and missed this. What is left: plan.md:91 does not make cluster ids part of the D4 spec, and it should. The key_error_rate parameter is over-built for a half-day function; a fixed caveat line does the same job. Also the Reynolds Cup paraphrase is slightly off: the page says entries inside the uncertainty are separated by stricter tie-break criteria (total clay bias, relative errors, number of missed or wrongly named phases), not left unranked.
verdicts.corrected_text: D4 spec: takes optional cluster ids and resamples clusters (powders, papers), never rows. When the key is flagged as draft or has known exceptions, print one line: "key not verified; no ranking claim". For the 40 scans a floor on key error now exists: at least 1 of 20 recipes has a documented off-recipe phase.

verdicts.target: P4 not_yet_relevant: homogeneity and stability lines for L2
verdicts.why: Correctly parked. The 0.3-of-tolerance homogeneity rule is confirmed by secondary sources in a search this run (the ISO text was not opened by me either). Nothing to do this month.

verdicts.target: P5 partly: no second-instrument subset; add "fixed scans, one instrument" to every headline
verdicts.why: The plan already states the limit three times (plan.md:55, :127, :198). The fix is three wording lines. It changes nothing the user does this month. Cheap and harmless; not a reason to pause.

verdicts.target: P6 partly: "harder" omits microabsorption, preferred orientation, non-crystalline content; add per-item tags
verdicts.why: Evidence checks out (plan.md:110, :142; builds.md:320; gaps.md:210). Scarlett 2002 did build samples for preferred orientation (brucite), non-crystalline content and microabsorption (search snippet; IUCr page 403). But those traps were chosen for a quantification test (how much of each phase). For a naming test the order of importance differs. A newcomer also cannot tag grain shape or crystallinity alone; those tags would be AI-drafted and need the specialist.
verdicts.corrected_text: For a naming exam tag, in this order: minor amount; weakly scattering phase next to a strongly scattering one (Li2CO3 beside La(OH)3 is the user's own 30-fold example); overlapping or same-structure pairs; poorly crystalline or non-crystalline ingredient; flat or needle grains; scan time. Only scan time and the heavy/light pairing are free for the 40 rows. The rest is an N3/L2 checklist, drafted by AI and checked at L1.

verdicts.target: P7 partly: declare a floor band below 1 wt%; misses there not counted against the tool
verdicts.why: The Leon-Reina numbers are confirmed (Zenodo record opened: detection limit about 0.2 wt% copper source, 0.3 wt% molybdenum; relative error under 20% only above 1 wt%). But that study used careful long scans. Its floor does not transfer to 2-minute scans, and "do not count" hides data.
verdicts.corrected_text: N3: report every band, including the lowest, with counts. Do not headline the lowest band. State the scan conditions beside each band. If a floor is declared, take it from that set's own paper, not from a different instrument.

verdicts.target: P8 violates: "No false-positive count appears anywhere" ... a lenient rule can turn an over-reported list into a correct scan; 1-2 hours; must fix
verdicts.why: Downgrade from "violates" to "partly". The published mark already punishes extras: the Dara paper counts a scan correct only if it "excludes any spurious phases", top answer only. The local lenient rule matches phases one-to-one (C16:31), which very likely also fails a scan with an extra phase. So the feared loophole probably does not exist in this marker. What is truly missing is one sentence confirming that from the code, and explicit missed/extra counts. The table already holds "true formulas" and "the program's formulas" per scan (plan.md:29), so the counts are a 15-30 minute addition, not 1-2 hours. The Reynolds Cup quote is confirmed verbatim: misidentified absent phases are "THE biggest source of bias".
verdicts.corrected_text: Add two integer columns (missed, extra) per rule, derived from the two formula columns already planned. Add one sentence after reading the marker code: "an extra phase makes the scan wrong: yes/no". For N3 report misses and extras per scan beside the all-or-nothing mark.

verdicts.target: P9 partly: hand-sort has no written rule; go/no-go has no preset number; five bins; ICSD numeric tolerances
verdicts.why: Pre-writing the sort rule and the threshold is proportionate: the decision gates 2-3 weeks of N1, and the user already pre-registers (builds.md:55; frozen PREREG). Two corrections. (1) Count in distinct formula pairs, not scans. The 40 scans come from 20 mixtures of only 10 ingredients, so one spelling such as "LaO3" for La(OH)3 repeats in every mixture that holds it. gaps.md:153 names three such spellings. Twenty differing rows may be 3-5 distinct cases. K must be in distinct pairs. (2) Five bins is one too many: a library gap mostly shows as "wrong under every rule", which is outside the differing-rows list. The ICSD numeric tolerances need crystal structures, which the stored results do not keep (plan.md:81), so that part belongs to N1 only.
verdicts.corrected_text: Before opening the data write: bins = spelling / real chemistry / key or recipe suspect / unsure (needs specialist). Decision = "build the reusable marker if at least K DISTINCT (true, named) formula pairs are real chemistry"; user picks K. Report both counts: differing rows and distinct pairs. Mark the sort "draft until L1".

verdicts.target: P10 partly: element list given or not; database date; 16% failed on database age
verdicts.why: Dara's abstract confirms it searches "within a given chemical space", so this is an elements-given exam. The 2002 search-match abstract (opened) confirms a two-stage design, first without chemistry and then with it, and says up-to-date databases are a condition of success. The specific 16% figure is not in the abstract and I could not verify it. The fix is one line on the task card.

verdicts.target: P11 partly: freeze one configuration, record its hash; "tools may have been tuned on" the round-robin scans
verdicts.why: The config-hash advice is fine but belongs to N3, which may never run. The audit missed the closer case of the same problem: the user's own lenient rule was tuned on these 40 scans. The hydrogen rule was added after seeing the misses and moved accuracy from 0.545 to 0.745 (gaps.md:153; C16:245). So 32 of 40 is an in-sample number for the marker. Also, Lutterotti 2019 (full text opened) says "Testing was done initially using the data set 1_h"; that supports "used as published test examples", not clearly "development examples".
verdicts.corrected_text: First-step table: add one line, "the lenient rule was adjusted after seeing these scans; its score here is in-sample". Any marker built from this table needs a check on compounds outside the 10 ingredients (the 20 reaction products, or the specialist's unseen pairs). N3 note: "scans public since about 1999 and used as test examples in tool papers".

verdicts.target: P12 partly: pipeline never run on an externally verified item; optional "paper's per-scan verdict" column; IUCr sample 1 positive control
verdicts.why: Right principle. Promote the optional column to a required one: the notes say the 38 and 35 are "the marks printed in the paper's own spreadsheet" (verify_K4_evidence.md:17), so per-scan published verdicts exist, and the paper states its marking rule. That column itemises the 6-scan gap at almost no cost. One number to re-check while doing it: the arXiv text as I read it says the commercial tool fails 2 of 20 at 8 minutes (18/20, so 34 of 40), while the notes record 19/20 (35 of 40). The off-recipe carbonate case may explain the one-scan difference. The IUCr positive control is a fair smoke test but only before N3.
verdicts.corrected_text: Required column in the 40-row table: the paper's own per-scan verdict, with the paper's rule quoted once. Reconcile 34 vs 35 for the second tool before quoting either.

verdicts.target: P13 partly: no "upper bound" wording; draw L2 recipes from real reaction-product phase lists; appeal-log columns
verdicts.why: The plan already says weighed sets are easy in three places (plan.md:142; gap G20; N3's deliverable "is it still too easy"). Only the "upper bound" sentence is new, and it is cheap. The recipe idea has a cost the audit skipped: many by-products of real reactions are not sold as pure powders. A lab would have to make and verify each one, which is the P2 problem again at larger scale. The Lutterotti 2019 case of a published key being contradicted (one lead oxide listed by the organisers, not found by the automatic run, confirmed absent by manual refinement) is verified and is a good reason for the three appeal-log columns.
verdicts.corrected_text: L2 and N5: "accuracy on weighed mixtures is an upper bound on accuracy on real products". L2 recipes: left-over starting chemicals plus by-products that can be bought as checked single-phase powders; say plainly that other by-products are out of scope. D1 CSV: add disputed-by / date / resolution.

verdicts.target: P14 partly: fresh items each round, key holder stays out (Reynolds Cup page)
verdicts.why: The four L2 lines are sensible and cost 15 minutes when L2 is drafted. "Standing means new powders every round" is the important point and it holds: it makes a standing exam much dearer than the 385-powder sizing. But two claims are credited to the Reynolds Cup page that the page does not state. It says one entry per organisation (confirmed) and that the previous winner has so far volunteered to organise the next round. It does not say the organiser may not enter, and it does not say mixtures must be fresh each round. Both are reasonable inferences, not quotes.
verdicts.corrected_text: Cite the page only for: one entry per organisation; winner organises next round; purity within 1 wt%; splits verified by XRD and XRF. Present "organiser's own tool reported outside the ranking" and "items retire once truth is released" as the plan's own rules.

verdicts.target: Direction 1: "The first step is the right kind of step" (low)
verdicts.why: Quoted lines are real (plan.md:19-43, :79-80, :91, :110, :127, :141). Checking the marker before trusting marks is the right order. The additions fit in about an hour if the task card is copied from the pre-registration and the Dara paper instead of being designed from scratch.

verdicts.target: Direction 2: "The plan puts its effort into scoring code and one line into the answer key" (high)
verdicts.why: Confirmed and strengthened. Reynolds Cup organiser rules are verified on the page. The Dara paper shows the weighed key already needed a judgement call on 1 of 20 recipes. The user's notes already hold two more key slips in this family of data (hydrate formulas, gaps.md:109; README says equal weight while file names encode 10-90 wt%, builds.md:565). For this month the cost is a wording change and one flag column. For L2 it changes what is asked of the lab, and makes "out of our reach" more likely.

verdicts.target: Direction 3: "The long-term aim is narrower than the plan thinks" ... open part = standing + hidden + third-party + naming-first + synthesis chemistry + written marking rule + multi-label score (high)
verdicts.why: Both papers are real and say what is claimed. Butler and Hillier 2021 (abstract opened): an automated algorithm picked phases from a 201-pattern library on 27 samples from nine contests and would have placed top three in all nine. Lutterotti 2019 (full text opened): automatic tool run on round-robin sample 1_h and on three of the four 2002 naming samples. Three corrections. (1) Both are after-the-fact runs by tool authors on public keys, for quantification in one case; they remove "machine-scored" from the novelty, not "hidden". (2) A novelty sentence with seven qualifiers is itself a warning. The honest open part is short: hidden and recurring, for software, on synthesis-type chemistry. The likely reason nobody runs one is the cost of fresh verified powders, not oversight. (3) Drop "multi-label score" from the open list: GALAXI already reports micro-F1 on phase lists, and the Dara paper already uses an all-present, no-spurious mark. The suggested alternative (offer scoring and a machine submission format to an existing body) is good advice for an ML person, but the fit is limited: the standing contest is clay minerals and quantification, and the IUCr round robins are over 20 years old. Another standing scheme the audit missed: ASTM C1365 qualifies cement X-ray analysis against certified reference clinkers (search result only, not opened).
verdicts.corrected_text: Novelty sentence: "Software has already been scored on contest weighed mixtures after the fact (2019, 2021). What still appears open is a recurring exam with hidden recipes for phase-naming software on synthesis-type chemistry. The main barrier is the cost of fresh, verified powders each round."

verdicts.target: Direction 4: "Weighed mixtures are the easy, less discriminating case" ... keep a small real-product arm with a consensus key (medium)
verdicts.why: The numbers are real (plan.md:165, :91) but the plan already knows this (plan.md:142; gap G20), so severity is low-to-medium, not a new finding. The "real-product arm with a consensus key" conflicts with the plan's own section 6 (no headroom: random 20.1% vs perfect 21.8%; single-rater labels) and with the user's core idea that the key should not rest on an analyst. The notes already hold the better version: a real-product set whose key is checked by a second kind of measurement (gap G21: about 12 weeks, about 200 hours, one outside lab). The audit did not link to it.
verdicts.corrected_text: Add the "upper bound" sentence. If a real-product arm is ever added, its key must come from a second measurement (chemistry or microscopy), not from analyst consensus. That is the existing G21 idea and is a later, lab-dependent item.

verdicts.target: Direction 5: "A diffraction person will not be surprised that formula-string marking is unstable" ... the multi-label score is where an ML-minded person adds something the older field lacks (medium)
verdicts.why: First half holds and the plan already says it (plan.md:151, :171). Dara itself clusters same-structure phases and groups similar compositions for display, so the tool's authors already handle this inside the tool. Second half is overstated: micro-F1 on phase lists is already in use (GALAXI 2026), the Dara paper has an explicit correct-scan rule, and the Reynolds Cup tie-break already counts missed and wrongly named phases.
verdicts.corrected_text: What an ML person can still add: a tested tiered matcher with a "cannot tell" outcome, intervals that resample powders, and a no-ranking rule when the key is unverified. Present N1 as "first runnable, tested rule card", nothing more.

verdicts.target: Direction 6: N4 omits the between-lab rung (about 6%, published round robin); compiled notes misread N4 (low)
verdicts.why: The rung is real: Alleno et al. 2015, one skutterudite specimen, 8 labs for the Seebeck coefficient, 6% (search snippet; PubMed page was a cookie wall). gaps.md:137 and :190 hold it. But it is a different statistic from the other rungs. It is a relative standard uncertainty at the 68% level, averaged over 300-700 K. The other rungs are median differences between pairs. For a bell-shaped spread a 6% standard deviation equals a median pairwise difference of about 5.7% (0.954 times the standard deviation; my arithmetic). I cannot check the side claim that earlier compiled notes misread N4; those notes are not in my files.
verdicts.corrected_text: N4 extra rung: "same specimen, different labs: 6% standard deviation, about 5.7% as a median pairwise difference; one material, 300-700 K; literature value". Give it an includes/excludes line like the others.

verdicts.target: Top change 1: 6-line task card plus pre-written five-bin sort rule and preset go/no-go number, about 1 hour
verdicts.why: Keep it. Fill the card from the frozen pre-registration and the Dara paper's stated rule. Add "top-ranked answer only". Use four bins. Set K in distinct formula pairs, not scans, because the 40 scans come from 10 ingredients.
verdicts.corrected_text: About 1 hour: copy the mark definitions onto a task card; write a four-bin sort rule; pick K as a number of distinct formula pairs; add the line that the lenient rule was tuned on these scans.

verdicts.target: Top change 2: log true, named, missed, extra per scan and rule; state whether marks punish extras; 1-2 hours
verdicts.why: Useful, but smaller and less alarming than stated. The published mark already fails a scan with any spurious phase, and one-to-one matching suggests the local mark does too. Two derived integer columns and one sentence from the code. 15-30 minutes.
verdicts.corrected_text: Add missed and extra counts and one sentence from the marker code. Also add the paper's per-scan verdict as a required column.

verdicts.target: Top change 3: stop calling weighed answers "certain"; use the 10 single-ingredient scans as the purity check; six L2 additions
verdicts.why: The wording change is plainly right and now has direct evidence from the same dataset. The single-scan purity check is too much for a newcomer in a stored-results-only step (an earlier checker said so). Replace it with a flag on the recipes the paper itself reports as off-recipe. What I changed. (1) P8 drops from "violates" to "partly": the published mark already fails a scan that names a spurious phase, and the local rule matches phases one-to-one, so the feared loophole probably does not exist; the fix is 15-30 minutes, not 1-2 hours. (5) The claim that a multi-label score is what ML adds is overstated; micro-F1 is already in use. (6) The seven-qualifier novelty sentence should be shortened; the real barrier is the cost of fresh verified powders. (7) The 6% between-lab rung is a different statistic from the other rungs and needs a conversion note.

Biggest miss. The audit never opened the body of the Dara paper. It defines the mark (top answer only, all weighed phases, no spurious phase) and documents a real off-recipe phase in one of the 20 recipes that the authors chose to leave out of scoring. That is direct evidence, on the user's own 40 scans, that a weighed key is not "certain" and does need a judgement. Two further misses matter for the first step: the 40 scans come from only 10 ingredients, so count distinct formula pairs; and the lenient rule was tuned on these same scans, so its score is in-sample. One direction-level miss: nobody has said how an exam should score "not sure", which is the user's own speciality.

Bottom line for the user. Yes, this is mostly eval work, of the kind ML calls meta-evaluation and metrology calls method validation. Yes, the one-off principles check was worth it. It does not justify a pause. direction_findings.claim: The overall direction is right. It matches where the materials-ML community's own criticism has gone, and the measured-data side has no equivalent yet.

A 2025 materials paper treats evaluation as measurement and proposes evaluation cards. A 2025 study shows most held-out-group tests are interpolation. All three are for computed data. The plan already passes or nearly passes 5 of 14 checks (P3, P8, P12, P13 follow; P1 nearly) and its cautions in plan/plan.md sections 7 and 8 are mostly acted on. challenge.lens: Adversarial check (stage 3) of the stage-2 audit written from the lens "evaluation work that already exists inside materials ML and autonomous labs". Local files read, read-only, all under <session-scratchpad> : plan/plan.md (all 213 lines), page/big-picture.html (lines 395-684), synth/gaps.md (lines 140-260 plus keyword search), synth/builds.md, synth/storyline.md, synth/glossary_usermodel.md (keyword search). Every plan.md / html / builds.md / gaps.md line number the audit quotes was checked and is real. Web pages I opened in THIS run: the Dara paper (arXiv 2510.19667 v1 and v2, HTML), Zenodo record 17410051 (landing page only), the Dara GitHub repo (scripts/, src/dara/, scripts/run_precursor_mixture.py, dataset/, dataset/README.md), arXiv abstracts 2512.18653, 2609.06908, 2308.14920 (abstract and full HTML), 2406.06489, 2503.10837, RADAR-PD HTML 2605.12478, PMC13470758, the KRICT-DATA/SIMD repo, and one university press release on a 2024 thermoelectric paper. All pages were read through a summarising fetch tool, so short quotes are as that tool returned them. Not opened: the RSC page for the noise-ceiling paper (403) and the Springer page (it redirected to a sign-in endpoint; I did not follow it). Nothing was written, downloaded, signed into or sent. I saw no instruction-like text in any page.

verdicts.target: is_eval_work: 'mostly' ... about two thirds of the items; D2 is data curation, D5/L3/L4/N6 are not eval
verdicts.why: The answer is right but undercounts. D2 asks whether files filed as measured are simulated or duplicated, and whether a duplicate sits on both sides of the user's calibration/test split (plan.md:85). In ML terms that is test-set contamination checking, which is evaluation work. D5, L3 and N6 are label-noise audits, and label noise caps any score. The plan itself lists 'Is the data what its label says?' as one of its four evaluation questions (plan.md:116). Only D0 (file rescue) is not evaluation. The audit's one-line name (benchmark auditing, not benchmark building) holds and is the most useful thing to tell the user.
verdicts.corrected_text: Yes. Every item except the file rescue is evaluation work in the ML sense: metric definition (D1, N1), splits and leakage (D3, N2), significance (D4), test-set validity and contamination (D2), label noise and best achievable score (D5, N4, N6), finding and running test sets (D6, N3, L2). It is auditing existing tests and your own scoring harness. Nothing in the next two months builds a new test.

verdicts.target: P1 partly: no by-formula row; 1-nearest-neighbour row on one split only; fix = add both, reword claim
verdicts.why: Evidence lines are real (plan.md:88, :107, :184, :188). The audit under-rates this row. Grouping by formula is what thermoelectric (TE) papers already do. I opened three: Barua, Salla, Kleinke 2026 use GroupKFold by composition on the Starry data set; Jia, Aziz, Hashimoto, Li 2024 use composition-based 10-fold cross-validation on 92,291 Starrydata2 points (press release opened); Na and Chang 2022 test on unseen material groups (repo opened; mostly on their own ESTM database, so the audit's 'on Starrydata' is loose). The plan's own breakdown says unseen formulas explain most of the 25.5 to 42.2 jump (plan.md:54). So the by-formula row is a kill test for the TE note, not a nice extra.
verdicts.corrected_text: In D3 run the by-formula split FIRST and print 1-nearest-neighbour under every split. Write the rule before running: if by-paper minus by-formula sits inside D4's interval, the field's existing habit already captures the effect, and N2 shrinks to the frozen list plus the ceiling. Cite Meredig 2018 (not re-opened), Jia 2024, Barua 2026, Na and Chang 2022.

verdicts.target: P2 violates: no split by publication year; 'design principle one of Matbench Discovery'
verdicts.why: True that the plan has no by-year split (my grep of plan.md and synth/*.md found none). But 'violates' rests on a wrong citation. I opened the Matbench Discovery full text. It does not split by time or publication year. Its first principle, 'prospective benchmarking', means test data come from a different generating workflow (element substitution, the WBM set) than the training data. Time splits are a drug-discovery habit, not a materials-ML consensus. Also, one TE paper already reports an out-of-time check on data released in 2023 (Jia et al. 2024). For TE a by-year split is a special case of by-paper with the same unseen-formula confound, and whether the on-disk table has a year column is unknown.
verdicts.corrected_text: Not a violation. Optional row in D3, only if a year column is already on disk. Do not cite Matbench Discovery for it. No network lookup for years.

verdicts.target: P4 partly: frozen list lacks a de-duplication rule and an allowed-training-data rule; 'ESTM is a subset of the same source'
verdicts.why: The frozen list is planned (plan.md:88). One factual error: ESTM is not a subset of Starrydata. It is a separate hand-collected TE database (Na and Chang 2022, repo opened) that overlaps in papers (gaps.md:162 counts shared papers). So the training rule must be database-agnostic. The de-duplication fix is not a 1-hour job. The list holds paper IDs. Cross-paper duplicates are curves re-plotted in later papers, and the notes' curve-only re-plot detector was refuted (builds.md:255). For a private list nobody else uses yet, more than two header lines is theatre.
verdicts.corrected_text: Two header lines, 15 minutes: (1) snapshot name and checksum; (2) 'any training row, from any database, whose paper ID is on this list makes an entry non-compliant; cross-paper re-plotted curves are NOT removed, count unknown'.

verdicts.target: P5 partly: XRD side never says whether an extra (spurious) phase fails the scan; fix = state the paper's rule above the table

It says a scan is correct if all weighed ingredients are found and no extra phase is reported. It does NOT say how a reported phase is judged to be 'the same' as the true one; the true reference entry for each ingredient was 'hand-picked by humans'. It also scores 'only the top solution' although the program returns several hypotheses. The notes do not say which hypothesis the user's marker scores.
verdicts.corrected_text: Above the 40-row table write three things: the set rule (all weighed ingredients found, no extra phase), which answer is scored (top one or any), and the sameness rule in use (strict string / lenient 0.10). Say for each stored mark which of the three it obeys. Add an 'extra phases' count per row. About 20 minutes.

verdicts.target: P7 partly: add found / missed / extra counts; micro precision-recall-F1 in N1; summed weight error in N3; 'sit beside' GALAXI micro-F1 0.935

missed: The plan's fork is mis-aimed. It says: if the differing rows are 'mostly spelling artifacts', treat it as a bug-fix for your own project (plan.md:25, :65). But spelling and hydrogen variants are exactly what others hit too. RADAR-PD built its LLM judge to tolerate 'hydrogen/hydration differences' and defect variants (opened). The Dara paper gives no sameness rule at all (opened). So 'mostly spelling' does not mean 'nobody else needs a marker'. The 40 easy scans can only size the effect in your harness. The case for a reusable marker rests on the tricky-pairs table plus this outside evidence.

The real unit in step one is the distinct (true answer, program answer) pair, not the scan and not the powder. The benchmark uses only ten ingredients (paper opened). One bad string such as 'LaO3' for La(OH)3 can flip many scans. Report how many distinct pairs cause the 12-to-32 swing. It may be three or four.

A number conflict nobody flagged. The arXiv text (v1 and v2) gives the commercial program 16 of 20 and 18 of 20, so 34 of 40. The notes, the page and D4's test case all say 35 of 40 (gaps.md:207, plan.md:91). One of them is off by one scan. Settle it when the supplement file is opened.

The notes already hold per-scan results from the paper's supplement (paired interval, errors by scan time, weight error 4.81 vs 5.49, per-answer spelling effects; gaps.md:154, :207; builds.md:194 'on disk'). The audit missed this and asked for a download. The right ask is to put that file on the read-only or rescue list.

'Weighed mixture = certain answer, needs no analyst's opinion' (plan.md:9) is slightly too strong. The recipe is certain. The phase in each bottle is not: the paper says the reference entry for each ingredient was 'hand-picked by humans' and checked against a scan of the single ingredient. Commercial powders can be hydrated or a different crystal form. This matters for the hand-sort now (the 'true formula' column comes from file names) and for the L2 lab request later (ask for single-ingredient scans).

Top-1 versus any-hypothesis scoring. Dara returns several candidate answers; the paper scores only the top one. The notes do not say which the user's marker scores. It is a metric choice like top-1 vs top-5 and belongs in the line above the table.

A third TE paper with grouped validation on the same source, plus an out-of-time check on 2023 data: Jia, Aziz, Hashimoto, Li 2024. It also reports R2 of about 0.90, which a reviewer will set against the plan's 42% median error. D3 should print R2 for a matching target or explain the difference.

The tricky pairs are chosen to break rules. Figures like 'strict disagrees on 8 of 18' are unit-test results, never error rates. The plan words this carefully (plan.md:78); N1 and N5 must keep doing so.

Fix budget. The audit proposes about 14 fixes. For step one keep five: the three-part rule line above the table, a pre-set threshold with an 'unsure' bucket, a mixture id, found/missed/extra under one named rule, and a distinct-pair count. Add the paper's verdict column if the file is on disk. That is about 2-3 extra hours on a 1-2 day step. Everything else rides with later items or is optional.
challenge.overall:
The audit mostly survives. Its line and file references are all real. Its answer to the user's question is right and can be stated more firmly: yes, this is evaluation work (every item but the file rescue), specifically benchmark auditing, and the check found no reason to pause. Proceed.

What I refuted or corrected:
1. P2 ('violates', add a by-year split) rests on a wrong reading of Matbench Discovery, which has no time split. Downgrade to optional.
2. P6 is right in spirit but wrong in three details. The per-scan results from the paper's supplement are, by the notes, already on disk, so no new download yes is expected. It is one column, not a gate. Per-row cause tagging is not feasible from stored formulas.
3. 'ESTM is a subset of the same source' is false; it is a separate database. The training rule on the frozen list must be database-agnostic.
4. The audit's TE rewording ('nobody groups by paper or by year') already fails: a 2024 paper on the same source uses composition-grouped validation and an out-of-time check. Safe claim: no one holds out whole papers, freezes a list, or prints a ceiling. The by-formula row becomes the kill test for the TE note.
5. Several fixes were sized too big for one newcomer (evaluation cards, de-duplication rule, 'not in pool' bucket). Shrunk above.

What the audit got plainly right: the set-level scoring rule must be written above the table; the hand-sort needs an 'unsure' bucket and a pre-set threshold; intervals must count 20 powders, not 40 scans; the TE task may be ill-posed, not just too easy; N4 and N5 should cite and apply.

What it missed, most important first: the plan's fork treats 'mostly spelling' as 'no one else needs this', but spelling and hydrogen variants are exactly what another group built an LLM judge to tolerate, and the tool's own paper gives no sameness rule and ships no scorer (all verified on the web). So the 40-row test sizes the problem in the user's harness; it does not decide whether the problem is real for others. Also: only ten ingredients, so count distinct answer pairs; and the paper text says 34 of 40 for the commercial program where the notes say 35.

Limits of this check: web pages were read through a summarising fetch tool; two sources were not opened (403, sign-in redirect); I could not look at the user's disk, so 'the supplement is already on disk' comes from the notes only.

is_eval_work.best_one_line_name_for_this_work: Auditing and repairing the exams for ML on measured materials data: the test items, answer keys, marking rules and splits. In short, evaluation-data curation plus exam auditing, with some eval-about-eval tooling on the side.
is_eval_work.which_parts_are_eval: 12 of 18 items. Test sets and answer keys: D1 (the 40-row marking test and the tricky-pairs key), D6 and N3 (harder public weighed sets as a practice exam), L1 (specialist check of the key), L2 and L5 (hidden exams). Splits and leakage: D3 and N2 (thermoelectric random split vs paper-held-out split, frozen list of test paper IDs). Statistics of comparisons: D4 (tie or not), and the '134-item test is a tie' critique of one company's claim. Metric design: N1 (tiered marker). Best achievable score: N4 (noise ladder). Commentary on evals: N5. Five of these are one level up, evaluation of evaluation: the D1 pairs table, D4, N1, N4, N5. These are the items closest to the user's stated focus, and the plan ranks all of them as 'courtesy', 'side deliverable' or 'lowest priority'. Note: evaluation DATA is itself curation (choosing, checking and documenting measured test items). The earlier decision 'evaluation data before a training corpus' (storyline.md:63) is a curation decision, not a departure from it.

The tool's authors name the real limits themselves (Dara paper, opened this run): phases absent from the database, disorder, and 'lab-diffractometer-based powder XRD cannot provide sufficient information about composition'. Reachable middle path: design the L2 ask as weighed mixtures that include non-ideal ingredients (a solid-solution member, a poorly crystalline powder, one ingredient absent from the reference library). verdicts.target: P2 Construct validity: 'partly'; weighed-mixture exam may not stand for the real job; fix = scope sentence + L2 mixtures with non-ideal ingredients
verdicts.why: The conclusion is right and rests on the tool authors' own words (verified this run: unknown phases, disorder, phases not in the database) and on the 2024 critique of the autonomous lab. But the audit's key evidence is misused twice. (1) '38 vs 35 tie, 15 vs 7 split' can be a ceiling effect (set too easy, which plan.md:142 already says), not a construct failure. (2) The 15 vs 7 comes from the key the audit itself calls contaminated in P5. It cannot be weak evidence in P5 and strong evidence here. Also missing: a weighed mixture is still a valid floor test. Failing it is informative (errors sit in the 2-minute scans, so headroom exists). Passing it proves little. The 'non-ideal ingredients' design is the audit's own invention with no source. A solid-solution ingredient re-opens the naming problem the balance key was meant to avoid.
verdicts.corrected_text: Keep the scope sentence. Add: 'Weighed mixtures are a floor test: failing is informative, passing is not proof.' Drop the tie-vs-split comparison as evidence. Pose 'non-ideal ingredients' as a question to the specialist or lab, not as a design.

Cells must allow 'unknown' and be filled only from what the dataset papers state. The probe is the best idea in the audit and is under-ranked as 'optional'. It is an open-set test (true phase missing from the library) with a certain key, on data already on disk, and it speaks directly to the user's 'not sure' project. Unknown: whether the user's frozen project plan already contains it (project not opened). It needs the user's yes to run the tool.

verdicts.target: P4 External validity before internal polish: 'partly'; 10-to-1 day count; fix = D6 on day 1-2, N3 before N1, N1 only if a second set agrees

'N3 before N1' is not proportionate: N3 needs a 1.87 GB download and unknown compute, while an internal marker fix is days. Bigger point the audit did not draw: the plan already HAS a second measured set, and there the rule moves only 1-3 of 20 (plan.md:165). By the audit's own gate, the reusable N1 is already unearned. And a second weighed set run with the same tool and library will repeat the same formula-string artifacts, so it is not independent evidence about marking.

verdicts.target: P5 Answer key independent of graded tools: 'partly'; footnote '11 to 13 of 20' as 'key made with the graded tool's suggestions; success = all peaks indexed'; make L1 blind-first
verdicts.why: Key provenance verified this run in the Dara paper: the expert worked 'incorporating the PDF-5+ database and suggestions from Dara'. But the footnote text is wrong for this number. '11 to 13' is the sessions' own re-mark (exact text 17 vs 4, composition 18 vs 7; plan/verify_K1_evidence.md:21 and :30; digests/C04-2of2.md:26) against the expert column. 'All peaks indexed' belongs to the paper's own 15 / 7 / 16 count. Blind-first is right, but marking 25 pairs from scratch is a bigger favour than 'where am I wrong?' and will lower reply odds. Also an internal conflict: the audit's P9 offers the tool's maintainers as a reviewer, which breaks this very principle.
verdicts.corrected_text: Footnote: 'Key = one expert's reading, made with the graded tool's suggestions in view. 11-13 = agreement with that reading under two text rules. It likely flatters the tool that helped write the key.' L1: send pairs without verdicts as tick-boxes (same / different / depends), about 10 minutes of work. Maintainers are fine for a bug report about formula strings, not for blessing the key.

verdicts.target: P6 Scoring rule must match the decision: 'partly'; fix = 'decision this distinction changes' column, drop tiers with no decision, add 'extra phases named' column
verdicts.why: The 'extra phases named' column is concrete and matters. The paper's mixture rule rejects spurious phases (verified). If the local marks do not, then 32 vs 38 compares two different rules. Keep it. The 'decision' column is not a desk task for a newcomer; an AI would fill it with guesses. The plan's tiers already map roughly to decisions (did the target form; which crystal form). A deeper point sits in the audit's own quote and is not drawn: lab XRD cannot pin composition, so 'Ni1.875O2 vs NiO' is not spelling. It is two library entries the scan cannot tell apart. The right rule is 'indistinguishable by this measurement', which formula distance cannot express.
verdicts.corrected_text: Keep the 'extra phases named' column in the 40-row table. Turn 'which distinctions change a decision?' into one of the questions for the specialist.

verdicts.target: P7 Effect must beat noise: 'partly'; MUST FIX before first step: written sorting rule, numeric threshold, 'recount', two independent sorts, extra columns
verdicts.why: Must-fix holds and is proportionate: 30 minutes against a 2-3 week build, and the assistant that proposed the kit also does the sorting. plan.md:33 ('reproduces 12, 17 and 32') against plan.md:164 ('quoted, not recounted') is a real conflict. Four changes. (1) Wrong unit. 40 scans are 20 powders scanned twice, and the notes list only 10 single-ingredient scans (gaps.md:208), so perhaps about 10 distinct ingredients. One library entry ('LaO3' for La(OH)3) can flip many rows. A threshold of '8 of 40 rows' can be hit by one compound. Count distinct (true compound, returned formula) pairs. (2) The plus-or-minus 12 point arithmetic is correct but aimed at the wrong quantity: the re-mark is deterministic on fixed outputs; the uncertainty is over compounds. (3) 'Two independent sorts': drop. The user cannot sort chemistry, and two AI passes are not independent. The 'cannot tell without a specialist' bin does that job. (4) The example thresholds are invented; the user picks.
verdicts.corrected_text: Before opening the folders, write: (a) unit = distinct (true compound, returned formula) pairs; rows reported beside it; count the distinct ingredients in the first hour. (b) three bins with a one-line reason each: same compound, different text / different compound / cannot tell without a specialist. (c) a threshold in distinct pairs, chosen by you first. (d) 'recount 12/17/32; any difference is a finding'. (e) columns: scan time, extra phases named; header: tool version, reference library, candidate cap.

The user's own project is about abstention, so accuracy-against-coverage reporting is almost surely in its frozen plan already (cannot check; project not opened). Two concrete points survive and both already live elsewhere: the 'extra phases' column (P6) and the scope note that the exam hands the tool the element list, so it tests closed-list search (P2; verified in the paper: users input 'elements that can exist in the pattern').
verdicts.corrected_text: Skip the per-eval gaming paragraphs until the L2 request is drafted. Keep the two concrete points under P2 and P6.
